audio.t: Good morning, Riverside Community College. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to enrol on the evening pottery course that I saw advertised in the library.
Of course. I'll just take some details. Can I have your name, please?
Yes, it's Daniel Marchetti. That's M-A-R-C-H-E-T-T-I.
Thank you, Mr. Marchetti. Now, there are two pottery courses. One is for experienced potters and the other is for beginners. Which is right for you?
Oh, definitely the beginners' course. I've never touched clay before.
Lovely. That class runs on Wednesday evenings.
Hmm, I'm busy on Wednesdays, I'm afraid. Are there any other days?
Let me check. Yes, there's a second group on Thursday evenings, and there are still a few places.
Thursday is perfect. What time does it start?
It was six o'clock until last term, but they've moved it to seven so that people can come straight from work. It finishes at nine.
That suits me better, thanks. How much does the course cost?
It's ninety-five dollars for ten weeks, but if you have a library card you get a ten-dollar discount.
I do have one. The number is four, eight, two, one, three.
Thank you. So that brings the fee down to eighty-five dollars. You can pay by card when you arrive at the first lesson.
Great. Do I need to bring anything?
All the clay and tools are provided, but you should bring an apron, because it gets very messy. Some people also bring a towel, but that's up to you.
OK. And where is the class?

In Room twelve, on the second floor of the Arts Building. Most people park in the main lot, but it's often full in the evenings, so I'd suggest the car park on Elm Street. It's only a two-minute walk.
Thanks, I'll do that. Is there a break during the class?
Yes, at eight o'clock, and a free hot chocolate is included in the fee.
Wonderful. Thank you very much for your help.

parts.instr: Questions 11-20. Listen to a talk about a community project and choose the correct answer.
parts.instrVi: Câu 11-20. Nghe bài nói về một dự án cộng đồng và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information evening about the Millbrook Community Orchard. My name is Helen, and I coordinate the project for the town council.

The idea began three years ago, when a group of residents noticed that the old tennis courts behind the library had been unused since the club closed. At first the council suggested turning the site into a parking lot, but over two thousand people signed a petition asking for something greener, and the orchard was the result.

We planted the first forty trees last autumn: apples, pears and plums. Most were donated by a local nursery, though we bought the cherry trees ourselves, since the nursery had run out. Next month we shall add a hedge of hazel and a small pond, which should attract the frogs and insects that help to pollinate the blossom.

Now, how can you get involved? We have three kinds of volunteer role. Gardeners come on Saturday mornings to prune, weed and water. They don't need any experience, because a retired fruit farmer, Mr. Okafor, shows beginners what to do. Tour guides take school groups around during the week, and for that we do ask people to complete a short safety course. Finally, we need people to manage the harvest day in October, when the fruit is picked and shared out.

Some of you asked about the fruit. Everything grown belongs to the community. Volunteers get first pick, but the rest is sold at the Sunday market, and the money buys tools. We decided against selling to supermarkets because we wanted the fruit to stay local. Please do not pick fruit at other times, since the trees are still young and could be damaged.

Finally, a word about funding. The council covered the cost of the fencing, but for the next phase we have applied for a grant from a national gardening charity. We'll hear in March whether we've been successful. If we are, we will build a covered area where classes can be held in bad weather. If not, we'll organize a sponsored walk in the spring, so please keep that date free.

items.vi: Khu đất trước đây là sân quần vợt cũ sau thư viện. Bãi đậu xe chỉ là đề xuất ban đầu của hội đồng.

parts.instr: Questions 21-30. Listen to two students talking to their tutor and choose the correct answer.
parts.instrVi: Câu 21-30. Nghe hai sinh viên nói chuyện với giáo viên và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your design project, the model footbridge.
Yes. Our brief is to build a one-meter bridge from wood that carries as much weight as possible, and we have to submit a report too.
We've been arguing about the shape. I'd like a truss, with triangles, but Leila prefers an arch.
Both can work. What do your tests show so far?
We tested small samples of three types of wood: pine, birch and balsa. Balsa was the lightest, but it snapped under surprisingly little weight.
Birch was the strongest but it's heavy and hard to cut, so we're going to use pine.
A sensible compromise. Now, the joints. In my experience, students rarely lose marks because the beams fail. It's the glue joints that give way first.
That's exactly what happened in our first test. We used ordinary white glue, and the joint slipped.
Try an epoxy, but only on the joints that carry the heaviest load, since it's expensive.
Should we test the whole bridge before the deadline? We can only use the laboratory press on two days.
Book it now. The technicians ask for a week's notice. And remember, the final load test has to be recorded on video, because the marking team wants evidence.
On the report, how much should we say about the designs that failed?
Quite a lot, actually. Many students hide their failures. Markers reward reflection, meaning what you changed and why, so I'd aim for about half of the report to cover that.
Is there a word limit? We were worried about three thousand words.
That's generous, and diagrams and tables are not counted, so use plenty of them.
We also have to give a presentation, don't we?
Yes, ten minutes in front of the class. The usual mistake is slides that are crammed with text. Use pictures and talk to the audience.
Leila is better at speaking and I'm better at the technical side. Should she do most of it?
No. Share it, because the examiners expect to hear from both partners.
Last thing. Could we use a 3D printer to make some of the parts?
You could, but you would have to declare it, and the brief is about wood construction, so I'd steer clear of it.

items.q: What was the problem with balsa?
items.vi: Balsa nhẹ nhất nhưng gãy khi chịu tải rất nhỏ.

items.q: Which wood have the students decided to use?
items.vi: Bạch dương chắc nhưng nặng và khó cắt, nên họ chọn gỗ thông (pine).

audio.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about bioluminescence, which is the production of light by living organisms. It is not the same as fluorescence, where an object absorbs light and glows back. Here, the light is made by a chemical reaction inside the body. In most cases this involves a molecule called luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase, and it is the enzyme that makes the reaction happen quickly.

The phenomenon is far more widespread than most people imagine. In the open ocean below two hundred meters, roughly three quarters of all animals can produce light, whether they are jellyfish, shrimp, squid or fish. By contrast, on land it is rare and is limited mainly to insects, fungi and a few worms.
Most of these sea animals glow blue. Green is found in a few species, and red is extremely rare. The reason is simple: blue light travels furthest through seawater, so it is the most useful signal.
Why glow at all? Researchers identify several main functions. The first is defense. A number of squid, when attacked, release a glowing cloud into the water and slip away in the confusion.
The second function is hunting. The deep-sea anglerfish carries a glowing lure above its mouth, which attracts prey close enough to catch.

The third is camouflage, and this one is truly clever. Many fish in the middle depths have rows of light organs on their bellies. They adjust the brightness to match the faint sunlight filtering down from above, so predators looking up cannot see their outline. This is called counterillumination.
Communication is another reason. Fireflies are the best-known example, since each species has a distinct pattern of flashes that the males use to attract a mate.
Bacteria offer a different case. A single bacterium produces almost no light, but when the population reaches a certain density, all of the cells switch on together. This is known as quorum sensing.

Now, applications. The luciferase reaction needs energy from a molecule found in every living cell, so it can be used to test for life. In food factories, a worker wipes a surface with a swab, and if there is any contamination, the sample glows.

Finally, there is interest in the future of lighting. Researchers have made plants that glow faintly by adding genes from bioluminescent fungi. At the moment the light is too dim to read by, but the work continues.

parts.instr: Reading Passage 1: Tiny plastics, large questions. Answer questions 1-13.
parts.instrVi: Bài đọc 1. Trả lời câu 1-13.

items.text:
A
Since large-scale production began in the 1950s, humans have manufactured well over eight billion tonnes of plastic, and a large proportion of it has been discarded rather than recycled. Plastic does not decompose in any useful sense; instead, it fragments. Particles smaller than five millimeters are classed as microplastics, and those below one micrometer are usually called nanoplastics. Some are made small on purpose, such as the microbeads that were once added to face scrubs, but most are secondary particles, shed when bottles, car tires and synthetic clothing wear down. Washing a single load of polyester laundry, for instance, can release hundreds of thousands of fibers into wastewater.

B
For years, scientists thought of microplastics mainly as a marine problem, and the images that shaped public concern were of turtles tangled in nets and seabirds with stomachs full of fragments. That picture changed when researchers began looking for particles in places where nobody expected to find them. Fibers were detected in mountain snow, in Arctic ice cores and in the air above remote villages. They were found in tap water, in bottled water, in table salt and in honey. A team led by the environmental chemist Marguerite Oyelaran concluded in a widely cited review that the average adult might swallow or inhale thousands of particles every week, although she cautioned that estimates varied by a factor of a thousand depending on the method used.

C
That caveat points to a serious difficulty: there is no standard way of counting microplastics. Some laboratories filter samples and examine the residue under a microscope; others use infrared spectroscopy, which identifies the chemical signature of each particle but cannot detect the very smallest ones. Contamination is a constant threat, because a stray fiber from a lab coat can be mistaken for a finding. In one notorious case, a study reporting particles in human blood was later criticized because the sampling tubes themselves had been made of plastic. Researchers now insist on blank samples and glassware, yet the results from different teams are still hard to compare.

D
What, then, do the particles do once they are inside the body? Evidence from cell cultures and animal experiments suggests several possible routes of harm. The smallest particles may cross the lining of the gut or lungs and enter the bloodstream. Their surfaces can trigger inflammation, and they can carry other substances: additives such as plasticizers that disrupt hormones, and pollutants or bacteria that cling to them in the environment. In 2022 the pathologist Tobias Wren and his colleagues reported plastic fragments in a number of tissue samples taken during routine surgery, and a later study associated the presence of particles in arterial plaque with a higher rate of heart attack and stroke. Crucially, however, association is not causation. Patients with less healthy lifestyles may simply have been exposed to more plastic through packaged food and similar sources, and the same lifestyle could explain their heart problems.

E
Toxicologists add a further complication, which is that dose matters. Laboratory experiments often expose animals to concentrations far higher than anything found in human surroundings, and they tend to use perfectly spherical beads, whereas real-world particles are irregular, weathered shards of many different polymers. The experiments therefore show what is possible rather than what is probable. Several researchers argue that this is no reason for complacency. Their reasoning is that exposure is rising, that the particles persist for generations, and that, by the time harm is demonstrated beyond doubt, the contamination may be impossible to reverse. Waiting for certainty, they say, is itself a decision with consequences.

F
Policy has begun to move ahead of the evidence. Several countries have banned microbeads in cosmetics, some cities now require filters on washing machines, and the European Union has restricted intentionally added microplastics in many products. Critics note that such measures address only a small share of the problem, since tire wear and clothing are far bigger sources. Meanwhile, individuals are offered a bewildering range of advice, from avoiding plastic chopping boards to drinking only filtered water. Most scientists say that the evidence for the value of such steps is thin, and that systemic change, such as redesigning products so that they shed less material, will matter far more than personal choices. What nearly all agree on is that the research gap needs to close quickly.

parts.instr: Reading Passage 2: How the brain reads. Answer questions 14-26.
parts.instrVi: Bài đọc 2. Trả lời câu 14-26.

items.text:
A
Reading feels effortless to those who do it well, which is precisely why it is so easy to misunderstand. Unlike speech, which children acquire through simple exposure, reading is a recent cultural invention, perhaps five thousand years old, far too young for evolution to have produced a dedicated brain system for it. Cognitive scientists therefore describe reading as a kind of 'recycling': learning to read persuades regions that evolved for other purposes, particularly object recognition and spoken language, to cooperate in a new way. Brain imaging has identified a small patch of the left visual cortex that responds specifically to written words in literate adults; in people who never learned to read, the same patch behaves differently.

B
The popular belief that fluent readers sweep their eyes smoothly across a line is mistaken. Eye-tracking studies, begun by the psychologist Hannelore Vik, show that the eyes move in rapid jumps called saccades, separated by brief pauses, or fixations, of around a quarter of a second. Information is taken in only during the fixations. Skilled readers do not fixate every word: short, predictable words such as 'the' are often skipped, while rare or long words attract longer looks. Only a few letters beyond the fixation point are seen in sharp focus, and the span extends in the direction of reading, which is why readers of languages written from right to left show the mirror image of this pattern.

C
Once the eyes have delivered the letters, the brain must decide what word they form. Early theories assumed that readers sounded out every word. Modern models propose two routes working in parallel. One converts letters into sounds, which is essential for new or unfamiliar words; the other recognizes familiar words directly as visual wholes, which is faster. In English, with its irregular spelling, both routes matter, since 'yacht' cannot be decoded by rule while 'blorp' can. Children who struggle with the phonological route are often diagnosed with dyslexia, and a large body of evidence shows that explicit teaching of letter-sound relationships helps most of them substantially, although it is no guarantee of fluency.

D
Comprehension depends on far more than decoding. Readers must hold the start of a sentence in working memory while they process its end, resolve pronouns, and infer what the writer has left unsaid. Here, background knowledge turns out to be decisive. In a well-known experiment, children who had been rated as poor readers, but who were football experts, were given a passage about a match; they outperformed good readers who knew little about the game. The finding suggests that comprehension is not a general skill that can be practiced in isolation but is tied to what the reader already knows, which is one reason why wide reading itself builds the capacity to read.

E
Digital reading has generated heated debate. Several studies report that people understand long informational texts slightly better on paper than on screens, an effect attributed to the tendency to skim on screens and to the lack of physical cues about where a passage lies within a text. Yet the gap is small, shrinks with experience, and largely disappears when readers are given time and told that they will be tested. The researcher Ines Calloway has suggested that the real issue is not the medium but the habits attached to it: screens are associated with quick, shallow tasks, so readers adopt a quick, shallow strategy without realizing it.

F
These findings have practical implications. Teaching reading well means attending to several skills at once: awareness of sounds, vocabulary, knowledge of the world, and the stamina to concentrate. Some educators now argue that the curriculum should deliberately build knowledge through topics studied in depth, rather than through a series of unrelated passages, so that comprehension grows cumulatively. Others caution that the evidence for this approach comes largely from short experiments, and that long-term classroom trials are still needed. What is not in dispute is that fluent reading is a remarkable feat: within a fraction of a second, patterns of ink are converted into meaning, and the process draws on almost every region of the brain.

parts.instr: Reading Passage 3: Why ancient societies fell. Answer questions 27-40.
parts.instrVi: Bài đọc 3. Trả lời câu 27-40.

items.text:
A
The word collapse conjures images of cities swallowed by jungle, yet archaeologists increasingly question both the word and the images. When the great Maya cities of the southern lowlands were abandoned between roughly AD 800 and 950, the Maya people did not vanish; millions of their descendants live in the region today. What ended was a particular political system, with its kings, monumental building and long-distance trade, rather than a population or a culture. Scholars therefore tend to prefer terms such as 'transformation' or 'reorganization', and to ask not why a civilization died but why a complex society simplified.

B
For much of the twentieth century, explanations were monocausal: invasion, disease, soil exhaustion and climate each had a champion. The best-known single-cause theory held that societies destroyed their own environment, felling forests and exhausting the soil until they could no longer feed themselves. A few cases seemed to fit. Yet when researchers examined particular sites in detail, the picture grew murkier. The inhabitants of a small Pacific island often cited as a textbook example of ecological suicide, it now appears, were undermined chiefly by rats carried in by the first settlers and by diseases brought by later visitors, not by reckless overuse alone. Single causes, historians now say, are the exception rather than the rule.

C
Climate evidence has transformed the debate. Cave stalagmites, lake sediments and tree rings now provide records of rainfall year by year. They indicate that a series of severe droughts struck the Maya region in the ninth century, that a long dry spell coincided with the fall of the Akkadian empire around 2200 BC, and that weakened monsoons preceded the decline of the Indus cities. Yet correlation must be treated with care. Droughts are common in history, and most societies survived them. Climate change seems best seen as a stress that exposed weaknesses that were already there, rather than as an executioner.

D
Those weaknesses were mostly social and political. Large, centralized societies became dependent on narrow systems: a single staple crop, a handful of trade routes, and a ruling class whose legitimacy rested on ritual promises to bring rain and good harvests. When the rains failed, the promise failed, and with it the authority of the rulers. The anthropologist Priya Nandakumar has described this as a 'brittleness trap': the more a society invests in elaborate institutions, the more it must keep investing merely to maintain them, so that it has little reserve for emergencies. Rising inequality, warfare among rival cities and intensifying competition between elites for resources made adaptation harder still.

E
Not every society was brittle. Some regions responded to the same pressures by dispersing into smaller settlements, switching crops, or moving towards rivers. In the Indus region, for example, population appears to have drifted eastwards, towards areas with more reliable rainfall, and towns shrank while villages multiplied. This was a loss of urban life, but it was also an effective strategy for survival. Such cases remind us that decline is not a single event but a spectrum of outcomes, including successful adaptation, and that the people who lived through it were active decision makers rather than passive victims.

F
The question of whether modern societies could suffer similar fates is often raised, and often answered too confidently. Optimists point to our scientific knowledge, global trade and ability to monitor the climate. Pessimists reply that today's economies are far more interdependent than any ancient state, so that a failure in one place can spread rapidly. Historians are generally cautious about drawing direct lessons: ancient societies differed in scale, technology and beliefs, and the evidence from them is fragmentary. Even so, many find in the past a useful reminder that societies are most vulnerable when their leaders cannot admit that their strategies have stopped working.

G
New technologies are also reshaping the evidence. Airborne laser scanning, which can map the ground surface beneath dense forest, has revealed networks of roads, reservoirs and house foundations around Maya cities that are far larger than anyone suspected, implying populations that were denser than once thought. Isotope analysis of teeth and bones shows who migrated and what they ate, and ancient DNA is beginning to trace how populations moved after the cities fell. Each technique raises new questions, and the old certainties about sudden catastrophe look increasingly out of date.

items.text:
The table shows average daily household water use, in liters per person, in three countries in 2000 and 2020.

Norland: showers and baths 48 (2000), 41 (2020); toilets 37, 29; laundry and dishes 30, 26; garden 25, 12; total 140, 108.
Eastvale: showers and baths 30, 34; toilets 22, 20; laundry and dishes 18, 21; garden 40, 45; total 110, 120.
Southmere: showers and baths 20, 22; toilets 25, 22; laundry and dishes 15, 18; garden 5, 8; total 65, 70.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares how much water people in three countries used at home each day in 2000 and 2020. Overall, Norland was the only country where consumption fell, while Eastvale and Southmere both recorded modest increases.

Norland started with the highest total, at 140 liters per person, and reduced it to 108 liters. The biggest drop was in garden use, which more than halved from 25 to 12 liters, and toilet use also declined noticeably, from 37 to 29 liters. Showers and baths fell from 48 to 41 liters, but they remained the largest category in 2020.

By contrast, Eastvale's total rose from 110 to 120 liters. Garden watering was by far its main use of water, climbing from 40 to 45 liters, and showers and baths and laundry and dishes also grew slightly. Only toilet use fell, by two liters.

Southmere used the least water in both years, although its total increased from 65 to 70 liters. Toilet use dropped from 25 to 22 liters, whereas every other category rose, with garden use showing the largest relative growth, from 5 to 8 liters.

In summary, Norland was the highest user in 2000 but became the lowest-growth country, and by 2020 Eastvale had overtaken it as the biggest user of water at home.

items.q: Some people believe that museums and art galleries should be free for everyone, while others think that visitors should pay an entrance fee. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
items.sample:
People disagree about whether public museums and galleries should charge visitors. In my view, entry should normally be free, although there is a case for charging for special exhibitions. This is my opinion, and I will explain why.

Those who support fees make a practical argument. Museums are expensive to run, since they must pay for security, conservation and staff, and governments have many competing demands on their budgets. Ticket income gives a museum a stable source of money, and it may also encourage people to value what they have paid for. A visitor who has spent twenty dollars is likely to spend longer in the galleries than someone who drifts in to shelter from the rain.

However, I believe the arguments for free entry are stronger. First, museums hold collections that belong to the public, and in many cases they were bought with public money. Charging people to see their own heritage seems unfair, particularly to low-income families, who may be the very people who would benefit most from an educational day out. Second, evidence from several cities that abolished fees suggests that visitor numbers rise sharply, and that many of the new visitors are young people and first-time visitors. Free entry also encourages shorter, more frequent visits, so that people can look at one room and come back another day, rather than feeling they must see everything to get their money's worth.

Nevertheless, the financial concern is real. A sensible compromise is to keep permanent collections free while charging for temporary exhibitions, which are costly to organize, and to ask for voluntary donations at the door. Many museums that follow this model report that donations and shop sales cover a large share of the lost income.

In conclusion, although a fee can help museums to balance their books, free access serves the wider purpose of education and cultural participation. I therefore believe that governments should fund museums and allow everyone to enter without paying.

items.q: Describe a skill that you learned and are proud of. You should say: what the skill is, how you learned it, who helped you, and explain why you are proud of it.
items.sample: I would like to talk about swimming, which is a skill I learned when I was twelve. Until then I was afraid of deep water, and I had even avoided school trips to the beach. My parents decided that it was time for me to overcome that fear, so they signed me up for lessons at the local pool. I learned mostly from a patient coach called Mr. Hung, who started with very simple exercises, such as breathing and floating, before moving on to proper strokes. My older cousin also helped me by practicing with me at the weekend, and he never laughed when I made mistakes. It took nearly six months before I could swim a full length of the pool without stopping. I am proud of this skill for two reasons. First, I had to beat my own fear, which was much harder than the physical side. Second, swimming has given me a lot of confidence, and now I can enjoy the sea with my friends, and I even won a small medal at a school competition last year.

items.q: Do you think schools should teach more practical skills, such as cooking or first aid?
items.sample: Yes, I think schools should teach more practical skills because many young people leave school without knowing how to cook, manage money or help in an emergency. These skills are useful throughout life, and they can be taught alongside academic subjects without taking too much time.
items.vi: Ủng hộ dạy kỹ năng thực tế ở trường, nêu lý do hữu ích.

items.q: Is it better to learn a new skill online or in a classroom?
items.sample: It depends on the skill. Online lessons are flexible and often cheaper, so they suit subjects like languages or computing. However, for physical skills such as swimming or playing an instrument, a teacher in a classroom can correct your mistakes immediately, which is hard to do through a screen.
items.vi: Cân nhắc học trực tuyến và tại lớp, kết luận phụ thuộc vào kỹ năng.

items.q: Why do some adults stop learning new things?
items.sample: Many adults stop learning because they have little free time after work and family duties. Others are afraid of looking foolish, since they lose confidence when they are beginners again. I think employers and communities could help by offering short courses at convenient times.

audio.t: Good afternoon, Lakeside Sailing Club. How can I help you?
Hello. I'm interested in your beginners' sailing course for adults.
Certainly. Could I take your name, please?
It's Colin Hartley.
And could you spell your surname for me?
Yes, it's H-A-R-T-L-E-Y.
Thank you. We run the beginners' course on Saturday mornings. There is a Sunday course too, but it's already full.
Saturday is perfect for me. What time does it start?
It used to start at eight thirty, but this year we've moved it to nine o'clock, so people have time to get changed.
Good. And how long does the course last?
Six weeks. Some people ask for eight, but six is enough to learn the basics.
How much does it cost?
The normal price is ninety-five dollars, but if you book before the end of the month you get ten dollars off, so that would be eighty-five.
That's good. Do I have to pay everything today?
No, just a deposit of twenty dollars. You pay the rest on the first day.
What kind of boats do you use?
Small dinghies, with two people in each one. The larger yachts are only for the advanced course.
And what should I bring?
Wear warm clothes. We provide life jackets and waterproof jackets. You might want sunscreen, but we sell it in the shop. The thing people forget most is a towel, so please bring one.
Right. And where do we meet?
At the boathouse, not the main clubhouse. It's next to the car park by the north gate.
Thanks. One last thing. My daughter would like to join later. How old does she have to be?
Fourteen. Younger children can join the junior club instead.
Perfect. Thank you very much.

parts.instr: Listen to a talk about a community orchard and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe bài nói về một vườn cây ăn quả cộng đồng và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to the annual meeting of the Marlow Green Orchard Project. I'm Hannah Costa, the volunteer coordinator, and I'd like to start by reminding you where we began.

Five years ago this land was a railway depot. When the trains stopped, it was fenced off and slowly became a dumping ground. The old school playing field is next door and the hospital garden is across the road, so people often think we took over one of those, but no. The council said it could not afford a playground here, but it did allow us to plant trees.

We planted forty trees in the first winter. We deliberately chose old local varieties rather than the modern ones you see in supermarkets. They don't look perfect and they don't store as well. But a nurseryman told us they have grown in this valley for two hundred years, and they cope with our wet springs and local diseases far better than newer types. Some of them are sweeter too, but that was not the main reason.

Today we have a hundred and twenty trees and about ninety volunteers. We don't work in teams or follow a timetable. Instead, each volunteer adopts a tree and looks after it all year, pruning it and checking it for problems. People love this, because they can watch their tree grow, and quite a few give their trees names.

Autumn is our busiest season. The main difficulty is not theft, which is what we feared at first, and it is not the wasps, although they are annoying. It is that so much fruit ripens at the same time that we cannot pick it all before it falls and rots.

So what do we do with the fruit? Volunteers can take home as much as they like. The rest used to go to the food bank, but they could only use fresh apples, so now we press the surplus into juice, and a local cafe buys it from us.
That income pays for our insurance, which is more expensive than you would expect. Nobody at the project receives a salary, and the hardware store donates our tools, so those are not a cost for us.

We also welcome school groups. The children learn to recognize different kinds of apple, but what their teachers value most is that they taste fruit straight from the tree, which many of them have never done.

Our next plan, for next spring, is to put two beehives at the far end of the site. We hope the bees will improve pollination, and one day we will have our own honey. A beekeeper from the town has offered to train us. We are not planning to buy the neighboring land, and a classroom would have to wait until we have more money.
If you would like to help, you don't need any experience. We provide gloves, but please wear strong boots, because the ground gets very muddy.
Our working days are the first Sunday of every month, from ten until one. You don't need to book or write to us. Just come to the main gate and ask for me. Thank you.

parts.instr: Listen to two students talking to their tutor and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe hai sinh viên trao đổi với gia sư và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, let's talk about your project on school start times. Ruth, remind me what made you choose this topic.

Well, my younger brother is fourteen and he is practically asleep at the breakfast table every morning. I'd read that some schools have moved their start from eight to nine thirty, and I wondered whether it really helps.
We looked at lots of articles, but most of them were opinion pieces. There were very few that actually compared results between schools.
Good, that's a clear justification. So what is your research question?
Whether a later start improves attendance and test scores, not just how tired teenagers feel.
Fine. And your method?
We contacted two schools. Brookfield School moved its start time last year, and Ashby School did not, so we are using Ashby as a comparison. We will compare the attendance records.
Sensible. Are you planning to use sleep diaries as well?
Yes, we were going to ask students to write down when they went to bed and woke up for a week.
I'd think carefully about that. Diaries depend on memory, and teenagers tend to overestimate how much they slept.
We also thought about sleep trackers that students wear on their wrists, but the schools said every parent would have to give written permission, and that would take months.
Then keep the diaries, but treat them as supporting evidence and be honest about their weakness in your report.
All right. We already have the attendance data. At Brookfield, attendance improved by three percent.
But test scores hardly changed at all. That surprised us.
Perhaps it shouldn't. One year is a short time, and scores depend on many things, such as new teachers or changes to the courses. What will you say in your conclusion?
That we can't claim a cause, only a link between the later start and better attendance.

Exactly. Now, about presenting the results. I'd suggest a table with the figures for both schools and a short written summary. Draw a graph for attendance only, because there is no point in a graph for test scores that stayed the same.
That sounds good. And the deadline is the fourteenth, isn't it?
It was, but I've moved it back by a week because of the exam timetable. So you now have until the twenty-first.
That's a big help. Thank you.

items.q: What made Ruth choose the topic?
options: Her brother is tired in the mornings
She read a book about sleep
Her own school changed its hours
items.vi: Em trai Ruth gần như ngủ gục bên bàn ăn sáng nên cô quan tâm đến chủ đề.

items.vi: Hầu hết là bài nêu ý kiến, rất ít bài so sánh kết quả thực tế.

items.q: What is their research question about?
items.vi: Họ muốn biết giờ vào học muộn có cải thiện chuyên cần và điểm thi không.

items.q: Why did they choose Ashby School?
options: It is close to the university

It kept its original start time
items.vi: Ashby không đổi giờ học nên được dùng làm trường đối chứng.

options: They take too long to write
items.vi: Nhật ký dựa vào trí nhớ và thanh thiếu niên thường ước tính quá giờ ngủ.

items.q: Why did they decide not to use sleep trackers?
options: Getting permission would take too long
items.vi: Mỗi phụ huynh phải viết giấy đồng ý nên mất hàng tháng.

items.q: What surprised the students?
items.vi: Điểm thi hầu như không thay đổi, điều khiến họ bất ngờ.

audio.t: Today I'd like to talk about suspension bridges, and in particular how engineers have solved the problems that they face.

The idea is very old. The earliest suspension bridges were rope bridges, and in the mountains of South America people twisted grass into thick ropes to cross deep valleys. Some of these bridges were rebuilt every year.

In the early nineteenth century, builders replaced rope with iron. At first they tried solid bars, but these were heavy and brittle, so engineers moved on to chains made of iron links, and chains carried the first great road bridges.

Modern bridges use something different. The main cables are made from thousands of individual wires, each about five millimeters thick. A thin wire can be made much stronger than a thick bar, so bundling many thin wires together gives far more strength for the same weight. The wires are made of steel, and in a large bridge the total length of wire could circle the Earth several times.

A bridge must also survive wind. In nineteen forty, a bridge in the state of Washington began to twist in a moderate wind and fell into the river a few hours later. Nobody was killed, but the disaster changed bridge design forever.

Today, before a long bridge is built, engineers test small models of its deck in a wind tunnel, where fans produce winds of different speeds and directions. The results have shaped the modern deck. It is no longer a flat, solid plate. It has a streamlined shape, rather like an aircraft wing, so that wind can slide past it smoothly instead of pushing it around.

The other enemy is rust. The main cables are wrapped tightly and painted, but to be safe some bridges go further and blow dry air through the cable all the time, because without moisture steel cannot rust. With this system, designers expect the cables to last for a hundred and twenty years.

Finally, inspection. Checking cables high above the water used to be dangerous work done by climbers on ropes. Now many inspectors use drones with cameras, which can reach every part of the structure safely and quickly. Next week we will look at how bridges are repaired. Thank you.

items.vi: Cầu dây đầu tiên dùng dây bện từ cỏ (grass) ở vùng núi Nam Mỹ.

items.text:
A
For about ten thousand years, farmers have been changing the plants they grow. Each season they saved seed from the best plants and sowed it again, and over many generations wild grasses became wheat, rice and maize. This method, known as selective breeding, works, but it is slow. Creating a new variety with a useful trait, such as resistance to a disease, commonly takes ten to fifteen years, because the wanted gene arrives in the plant together with thousands of unwanted ones, which must then be removed through repeated crossing. In the twentieth century, breeders tried to speed things up by exposing seeds to radiation or chemicals that scramble the DNA at random, and then searching through thousands of seedlings for a lucky improvement. From the 1990s, genetic modification offered a more direct option: moving a gene from one species into another. It was powerful, but it also provoked a public debate that continues today.

B
Gene editing is a different approach. The best-known tool, called CRISPR, can be compared to a pair of molecular scissors with a built-in address. Scientists give it a short guide sequence that matches one particular spot in a plant's DNA, and the scissors cut only there. The plant's own cells then repair the break, and they often make a small mistake while doing so, which switches the targeted gene off. If the aim is simply to disable a gene, no foreign DNA needs to remain in the finished plant. Many of the resulting changes are indistinguishable from the mutations that occur naturally, every day, in every field.

C
The first results are now arriving. A team at the Halden Institute in the northern highlands edited three copies of a gene in bread wheat that normally help a mildew fungus to enter the leaf. The edited plants stayed healthy when exposed to the disease, and the farmers who trialed them needed fewer chemical sprays. Elsewhere, a rice variety has been edited to take up less of the toxic metal cadmium from contaminated soil, and a tomato has been altered so that its fruit stays firm for longer after picking, which reduces waste during transport. None of these projects added genes from other species.

D
Cost and speed may matter as much as the science. A disease-resistant variety that once took twelve years can sometimes be produced in three or four, and the equipment needed costs a small fraction of what a large biotechnology project requires. Getting a genetically modified crop approved has often cost tens of millions of dollars in safety trials, a sum that only big companies could afford. Because editing is cheaper, universities and public laboratories in lower-income countries have started to work on local crops such as cassava, sorghum and banana, which have never attracted much commercial investment.

E
Regulation, however, is uneven. Some countries treat an edited plant that contains no foreign DNA as equivalent to a conventionally bred one and approve it through a light procedure. Others apply the same strict rules that cover genetically modified crops. This difference creates problems for trade: because no test can tell an edited change from a natural mutation, inspectors have no way to check which rules a shipment of grain ought to follow. Critics raise further concerns. They point out that the scissors sometimes cut at the wrong place, producing "off-target" changes, and although careful screening can find most of these, no test is perfect. Others worry that a handful of companies will own the patents on the key techniques, and that consumers will have little information about what they are eating.

F
Scientists themselves are cautious about the hype. The traits farmers value most, such as yield and tolerance to drought, are usually controlled by hundreds of genes acting together, not by a single gene that can be switched off. Editing such traits remains far harder than blocking a fungus. Most researchers therefore see gene editing as an addition to traditional breeding rather than a replacement for it. Better soil management, careful water use and crop rotation will still matter, and a clever edit will not make up for neglect of these basics. What the technology does offer is a faster, cheaper way to fix specific problems, at a time when climate change is bringing new pests and harsher weather to farms everywhere.

items.text:
A
Traditional economic theory describes people as rational calculators who weigh costs and benefits carefully, know what they want and never let mood or habit interfere. One economist joked that such people belong to a different species, which he called "Econs", and that real human beings are more like confused travelers. Over the past fifty years, psychologists and economists have collected evidence that supports the joke. Real people use mental shortcuts, are strongly affected by how a choice is presented, and often act against their own long-term interests. The field that studies these patterns is called behavioral economics.

B
Several patterns have been observed again and again. The first is loss aversion: a loss feels roughly twice as painful as an equal gain feels pleasant. In a well-known experiment, students who were given a coffee mug asked for far more money to sell it than other students were willing to pay to buy the same mug. The second is anchoring. When charities suggest a donation amount on a form, the average gift rises or falls with the number suggested, even though donors believe they decided for themselves. A third pattern is present bias, which is the preference for a small reward now over a larger one later. It helps to explain why so many people save too little for retirement, even when they understand the arithmetic perfectly.

C
These discoveries led to the idea of the nudge. A nudge is a small change in the way choices are presented that steers people toward better decisions without forbidding any option or changing the financial incentives. The person who arranges the choices is called a choice architect, and since every choice has to be presented somehow, supporters argue that everyone who designs a form or a menu is already an architect, whether they intend to be or not. In one example, a school canteen in the town of Lindholm moved fruit to eye level beside the till and placed sweets in a less visible spot. Nothing was banned, yet fruit sales rose by a quarter.

D
Defaults are among the most powerful nudges. In one company, employees originally had to fill in a form in order to join the pension scheme, and about forty percent did so. When the company changed the rule so that everybody was enrolled automatically unless they chose to leave, participation rose above ninety percent. Countries in which citizens are organ donors unless they opt out have much higher registration rates than countries in which people must opt in. People stay with the default for two reasons: inertia, since changing it takes effort, and a feeling that the default must be what experts recommend.

E
Another group of nudges relies on social norms. In one trial, households received letters that compared their electricity use with that of their neighbors. Those that used more than the average cut their consumption, though only by about two percent. Hotel cards that tell guests that most visitors reuse their towels have a similar effect. The change for each person is small, but when the message reaches millions of households, the combined saving can be larger than that from an expensive information campaign.

F
Nudges have critics, and some of their criticism is fair. A review of many trials found that the typical effect was modest, and that studies carried out by academics reported larger effects than those carried out by governments, partly because striking results are more likely to be published. The effect of some nudges also fades once they are withdrawn. Others argue that nudges treat symptoms, and that big problems such as obesity or pollution need laws and taxes. A further objection is ethical: steering people without their knowledge looks like manipulation. Supporters reply that choices are always arranged in some way, so the real question is who designs the arrangement, and for what purpose. One test they suggest is transparency: a nudge is acceptable if it would still work after people had been told about it.

G
More recently, attention has turned to the opposite problem, which has been named sludge. Sludge is unnecessary friction that makes good choices harder, such as a long form that discourages people from claiming a benefit they are entitled to, or a subscription that is easy to start and almost impossible to cancel. Organizations that review their procedures and remove sludge may do more good than those that simply add new nudges. Behavioral economics, in other words, is less a collection of tricks than a way of looking at the gap between how we imagine people behave and how they really do.

items.text:
A
Every concert hall is a musical instrument, and a very large one. The same orchestra playing the same piece can sound rich and glowing in one building and thin and muddy in another, and the difference lies entirely in the hall. Until about 1900, designers had no way of predicting this. They built new halls by copying successful ones, and when a hall turned out well, much of the credit belonged to luck. Several famous nineteenth-century halls still admired today were built this way, and many others that nobody remembers were built the same way and failed.

B
The first scientific approach came from a young physicist named Wallace Sabine. In 1895 he was asked to improve a university lecture room in which speech was hard to understand. With an organ pipe and a stopwatch, he measured how long a sound took to die away after the pipe was switched off, and he repeated the measurement night after night, carrying seat cushions in and out of the room to see what difference they made. He discovered that this time, now called the reverberation time, grows with the volume of a room and shrinks as the total amount of absorbing material increases. His simple formula is still taught today, and it turned acoustics from guesswork into a science.

C
The best reverberation time depends on what the room is used for. A hall for speech needs less than one second, because longer echoes blur the consonants that make words clear. Opera, in which the words matter but the singing needs support, works best at about 1.3 to 1.6 seconds, and symphonic music usually needs about 1.8 to 2.2 seconds. A long reverberation gives music warmth and fullness, because each note blends into the next. However, it can also make fast passages sound smeared, which is why music from the eighteenth century, with its quick and delicate lines, often sounds better in a drier room.

D
The shape of the hall matters as much as its reverberation. Many of the best-loved halls, such as those in Vienna and Boston, are tall, narrow rectangles known as shoebox halls. Because the side walls are close to the listeners, some of the sound bounces off them and arrives at the ears a fraction of a second after the direct sound, from the side. The brain interprets these early side reflections as a sense of being surrounded by the music, which musicians call spaciousness. In the 1960s, a hall in Berlin tried a different idea: the audience was seated on terraces around the orchestra, like the rows of a vineyard on a hillside, so that more people sat close to the stage. The result was a feeling of closeness, but the side walls were far away, so the designers had to add large reflectors above the stage to restore the missing early reflections.

E
Audience members affect the sound, too. A human body absorbs sound far better than a hard wooden seat, so a full hall can have a much shorter reverberation time than an empty one. This creates a problem for orchestras, who rehearse in an empty hall and then perform in a full one. To solve it, designers cover the seats with fabric and padding chosen so that an empty seat absorbs about as much sound as a seat with a person in it. The rehearsal then sounds nearly the same as the concert. The walls matter as well: heavy plaster and thick wood reflect deep notes well, while thin panels soak up the bass and leave a hall sounding weak.

F
Not every hall is used only for symphonies. Many have to host amplified pop concerts, lectures and opera, all of which need different conditions. One answer is variable acoustics: heavy curtains that slide out of the walls, ceilings that can be raised or lowered, and panels that rotate to show either a reflecting or an absorbing face. Before building starts, designers now test their ideas with computer simulations and with scale models, in which they use higher-pitched sounds to match the smaller size. Yet computers still cannot fully predict how a hall will feel to a listener, and many consultants admit that the final judgment must come from careful listening in the finished room.

G
Halls do fail, even today. Several buildings opened in the twentieth century to great expectations were criticized by musicians and critics for weak bass or harsh sound, and at least one was rebuilt inside after only a few years. Performers also learn to adjust. A conductor in a very resonant hall may take a slow passage a little slower and shorten the silences between phrases, while in a dry hall the tempo may be a little quicker. The lesson is that a hall is not a machine for producing sound but a partner for the musicians, and a good one needs to be matched to the music that it is built to serve.

parts.instr: You should spend about 20 minutes on this task. Write at least 150 words.
parts.instrVi: Task 1: dành khoảng 20 phút, viết ít nhất 150 từ.

items.text:
The table shows the percentage of commuters in the city of Dunmere who used five different ways of travelling to work in 2000 and in 2020.

Car: 62 percent (2000), 48 percent (2020)
Bus: 20 percent (2000), 18 percent (2020)
Train: 8 percent (2000), 15 percent (2020)
Bicycle: 4 percent (2000), 11 percent (2020)
Walking: 6 percent (2000), 8 percent (2020)

Note: a new cycle lane network opened in Dunmere in 2012.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares how commuters in Dunmere travelled to work in 2000 and 2020. Overall, the car remained the most popular choice, but its share fell noticeably while the train and the bicycle became much more common.

In 2000, the car dominated, accounting for 62 percent of commuters, more than three times the figure for the bus, which stood at 20 percent. By 2020, the car share had dropped to 48 percent, a fall of 14 percentage points, although it was still far ahead of every other method. The bus also declined, but only slightly, from 20 to 18 percent.

In contrast, the train and the bicycle gained ground. The proportion using the train almost doubled, rising from 8 to 15 percent. The bicycle showed the sharpest relative increase, from just 4 percent to 11 percent, which is nearly three times as high. This growth may be linked to the cycle lanes that opened in 2012. Walking changed least, going up from 6 to 8 percent.

In summary, the pattern shows a gradual move away from the car toward rail and cycling, while the bus and walking stayed relatively stable.
items.vi: Task 1: nêu xu hướng chung (ô tô giảm, tàu và xe đạp tăng), so sánh số liệu năm 2000 và 2020, không đưa ý kiến cá nhân.

parts.instr: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
parts.instrVi: Task 2: dành khoảng 40 phút, viết ít nhất 250 từ.

items.q:
In many countries, more and more people now work from home for at least part of the week.

Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
items.sample:
Working from home was once rare, but it has become a normal part of life for millions of employees. In my opinion, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that companies and workers manage the change carefully.

The most obvious advantage of working from home is the time and money saved. A person who no longer travels for an hour each way gains two hours a day, which can be used for exercise, family or rest. Employers also benefit, because they can rent smaller offices, and many studies suggest that staff who control their own schedules are often more productive. In addition, working from home allows people who live far from big cities, or who have health problems, to take jobs that were once closed to them. There is also an environmental gain, since fewer commuters mean less traffic and pollution.

However, there are real disadvantages. Some people feel isolated when they spend whole days alone, and they miss the casual conversations that often lead to new ideas. Young employees in particular may learn more slowly, since they cannot watch experienced colleagues at work. Another problem is that the border between work and private life becomes blurred, so that people answer emails late at night and find it difficult to switch off. Not everyone has a quiet room at home either, and this makes concentration hard.

These problems can be reduced, though. Many companies now ask staff to come to the office two or three days a week, which keeps the social contact while saving most of the travel. Clear rules about working hours can also protect personal time.

In conclusion, although working from home has weaknesses, a flexible mixture of home and office work offers more benefits than drawbacks, and I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

items.sample: Yes, I enjoy cooking, especially on weekends when I have more time. My grandmother taught me to make simple soups, and I like it because it is relaxing and I can share the food with my family.
items.vi: Part 1 về nấu ăn: trả lời có/không, nêu người dạy và lý do.

items.q: What kind of weather do you like best, and why?
items.sample: I like sunny weather best, because I can spend more time outside with my friends. In the summer, we often go to the beach. When it is rainy, I feel sleepy and prefer to stay at home.
items.vi: Part 1 về thời tiết: nêu loại thời tiết thích nhất và lý do.

items.q: Do you like reading? What kind of books do you usually read?
items.sample: Yes, I do. I usually read adventure novels and sometimes books about history. I like reading before I go to bed, because it helps me relax, and I learn new things from the books too.
items.vi: Part 1 về đọc sách: nêu thể loại sách và lý do.

items.q: How do people celebrate public holidays in your country?
items.sample: In my country, people celebrate public holidays mostly with their family. They prepare special food, visit relatives and often travel back to their hometowns. Streets are decorated, and there are fireworks in the big cities.
items.vi: Part 1 về ngày lễ: mô tả cách mọi người ăn mừng.

parts.instr: Part 2: Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2: nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a skill that you learned and that was difficult at first. You should say: what the skill was, how you learned it, why it was difficult at the beginning, and how you feel about it now.
items.sample: I would like to talk about learning to play the guitar, which was one of the most difficult skills I have ever tried to learn. I started about three years ago, when my uncle gave me an old guitar as a birthday present. At first, I could not play anything at all, and my fingers hurt after only ten minutes. I learned mainly from online videos, and I also practiced with my cousin, who already played quite well. The hardest part was changing quickly between chords, because my fingers did not know where to go, and the sound was often terrible. Several times I wanted to give up, but my cousin told me that everyone struggles in the beginning, so I decided to practice for twenty minutes every day. After about three months, I could play a simple song from beginning to end, and I felt very proud. Now I can play many songs, and I sometimes perform for my family. I feel that learning the guitar taught me patience, and I am glad that I did not stop when it was difficult.
items.vi: Part 2: kể kỹ năng đã học, cách học, khó khăn ban đầu và cảm xúc hiện tại; bám theo cả bốn ý trên thẻ.

parts.instr: Part 3: Discuss more abstract questions related to the Part 2 topic.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3: thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng liên quan đến chủ đề phần 2.

items.q: Do you think people learn skills better at school or by themselves? Why?
items.sample: I think both ways are useful, but it depends on the skill. At school, students get clear guidance from teachers and a fixed plan, which is good for basic subjects. However, people often learn practical skills better by themselves, because they can choose the speed and practice as much as they want.
items.vi: Part 3: so sánh học ở trường và tự học, nêu lý do và nhượng bộ.

items.q: How might technology change the way people learn new skills in the future?
items.sample: I believe technology will make it easier to learn almost anything in the future. People can already watch lessons online, and programs can give instant feedback. In the future, virtual reality may let learners practice difficult jobs safely, so more people will be able to learn new skills at home.
items.vi: Part 3: dự đoán ảnh hưởng của công nghệ đến việc học kỹ năng.

items.q: Some people say that adults should keep learning throughout their lives. Do you agree?
items.sample: Yes, I agree that adults should keep learning. The world changes quickly, and jobs that exist today may disappear, so new skills are very important. Learning also keeps the mind active and gives older people a sense of purpose, and it can be a pleasure rather than a duty.
items.vi: Part 3: nêu quan điểm về việc học suốt đời, đưa lý do và ví dụ.

Hello. I saw your poster about the beginner courses and I'd like to book a place.
Certainly. Can I have your name, please?
Yes, it's Tom Lindqvist.
Could you spell your surname for me?
Of course. L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T.
Thank you. And a contact number?
It's 555 0174. Oh, sorry, I mean 0147.
0147. Got it. Now, we offer two courses. One is a river course, and the other is a coastal touring course on the open sea. The river course is calmer, of course.
I've paddled on rivers before, so I'd like to try the coastal one.
The coastal touring course, then. The next one starts on Saturday the fourteenth of June. There is another one in July, but it's already full.
June is perfect. Where do we meet?
Everyone meets at the boathouse at half past eight. Please don't go to the main office, because it's on the other side of the harbor.
The boathouse, OK. How much does the course cost?
It's ninety dollars normally, but there's a discount for new members, so it's eighty-five dollars for you.
That's good. What do I need to bring?
The equipment is included: a life jacket, a paddle and a helmet. But you should bring a towel and a change of clothes, because you will probably get wet.
No problem.
Lunch is provided as well. Do you have any food allergies?
Yes, I'm allergic to peanuts.
I'll tell the kitchen. One last thing: we take a maximum of eight people in each group, so you'll get plenty of attention.
Great. Thank you very much.
You're welcome. See you in June.

parts.instr: Listen to a talk about volunteering at a nature reserve and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe bài nói về việc làm tình nguyện tại một khu bảo tồn thiên nhiên và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information session about volunteering at the Marsh Lane Wetland Reserve. My name is Helena, and I'm the volunteer coordinator.

Let me begin with a little history. The reserve opened twelve years ago on land that used to be a garbage dump. Local residents spent two years persuading the council to turn it into a nature reserve, and the first volunteers planted reeds along the water's edge. Today it covers about ninety hectares and is home to more than two hundred species of birds.

Many people assume that volunteers spend all their time counting birds. In fact, the most common task is managing the water level. In summer the channels fill with weeds, and unless we clear them, the water becomes stagnant and the fish die. So on Tuesdays our team works in waders, cutting back the weeds. If you prefer to stay dry, on Thursdays we repair paths and boardwalks, and on Saturdays we run the visitor center and lead school groups.

Before you start, you'll need to attend a half-day training session. We run these on the first Sunday of every month. You'll learn about safety around deep water, how to recognize protected plants and how to use the tools. We ask all new volunteers to commit to one session every two weeks for six months, because it takes time to learn the work and the training is expensive for us.
The reserve provides boots, gloves and waterproof jackets, but please bring your own lunch. There's a small cafe, but it only opens on weekends.

This year we have a special project: building a new bird-watching hide on the north side. The old one was damaged in a storm last winter, and it was always too small for school groups. The new one will hold thirty people, and its design includes a ramp so that visitors in wheelchairs can use it. We've raised most of the money, but we still need about four thousand dollars, so next month we're holding a sale of plants and secondhand books. We did think about a sponsored walk, but we felt a sale would bring in more.

Finally, a word about wildlife. Please don't expect to see otters. They're shy and mostly come out at night. But if you're patient, you'll almost certainly see kingfishers by the main channel in the early morning.

If you'd like to sign up, please don't fill in the paper forms on the table, because we're switching to an online system. Just scan the code on the poster by the door. Thank you, and I hope to see some of you on the reserve soon.

parts.instr: Listen to two students talking to their tutor about a research project and choose the correct answers.
parts.instrVi: Nghe hai sinh viên trao đổi với gia sư về một dự án nghiên cứu và chọn đáp án đúng.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to discuss your project on phone notifications and concentration.
Yes, Dr. Hughes. We've been planning the experiment, but we're not sure about the number of participants.
We were thinking of using sixty students, but we only have three weeks to collect the data.
Sixty is ambitious. For a small student project, forty would be enough, twenty in each group, as long as the groups are chosen at random.
OK, we'll go with forty. The next question is the task. We thought of giving them a long math test, but Ravi thinks it would be too stressful.
I think some people would be anxious about math, and that would affect the results more than the notifications would.
A good point. What else could you use?
A proofreading task, perhaps? Participants find spelling mistakes in a printed article.
That's much better. Everyone can do it, and the result is easy to measure, because you simply count the errors they miss.
For the notification group, we'll send text messages to their phones during the task.
How many messages?
Six in fifteen minutes, at regular intervals.
That might feel a little artificial. Most people get messages unpredictably, so I would send them at random times instead. Six is fine.
Good idea. Now, where should we run it? The psychology lab is booked until next month.
Then use a study room in the library. Students can reserve them for free, and it's a more realistic place to study anyway.
One problem is that most of our participants will be first-year psychology students, because they get course credit for taking part.
That's a limitation. It doesn't make the study worthless, but you must mention it in your discussion, and be careful not to claim that your results apply to everyone.
What about ethics? Do we need approval?
Yes. The committee meets next Wednesday, so you must hand in the form by Monday. Don't leave it until Friday.
We'll also need a consent form. Should we tell participants the real purpose of the study at the beginning?
If they knew you were studying notifications, they would watch their phones all the time. So tell them it's a study of proofreading, and explain the real aim afterward, in a debriefing.
We were also going to do a pilot test first, with a couple of friends.
Definitely. It will show you whether the timing and the instructions work before you start the real experiment.
And what about the report? Ravi wants to start with the results.
Always begin with an introduction that reviews earlier research, so the reader knows why your question matters. Starting with the results is a common mistake.
Is it all right to put the graphs in an appendix?
I'd put the main graph in the results section. Readers shouldn't have to turn to the end of the report to find your key finding.
Thank you, that's really helpful.

audio.t: Good morning. Today I'm going to talk about the history of the lighthouse, and how a simple idea developed into a sophisticated piece of engineering.

The most famous lighthouse of the ancient world was the Pharos of Alexandria, which was completed around 280 BC. Estimates of its height vary, but most historians believe it was about one hundred meters tall, which made it one of the tallest structures in the world for many centuries. At night a fire burned at the top, and its light may have been reflected out to sea by sheets of polished bronze.

After the fall of the Roman Empire, many coastal lights went out. In medieval Europe, the few that survived were often kept by monks, who lit beacons on cliffs and headlands as an act of charity for sailors. The fuel was usually wood, and later coal, which burned for longer but produced a great deal of smoke that blackened the glass of the lantern.

Real progress came in the eighteenth century. Early towers built on rocks in the open sea were repeatedly destroyed by storms. In 1750 an engineer named Walter Greaves built the Grayrock Lighthouse using blocks of granite cut so that they locked into each other like the pieces of a puzzle. The blocks were joined with what are known as dovetail joints, and the tower stood for over a hundred years.

The next breakthrough was optical. In the 1820s, a French physicist designed a lens made of concentric rings of glass prisms. It could bend the light from a small lamp into a powerful beam, and it was far lighter than the solid lenses that had been tried before. Light from these lenses could be seen from more than thirty kilometers away.

A lighthouse keeper's life was hard. Keepers took turns to watch the light all night, and they had to climb the stairs every few hours to wind up the clockwork mechanism that turned the lens. If a keeper forgot, the beam stopped sweeping and ships could no longer recognize the light. In fog, light was no use at all, so many stations also had a foghorn, which replaced the old system of ringing a bell.

During the twentieth century, electricity changed the work. Automatic systems were introduced in the 1960s, but they were installed slowly, and even in 1990 about a quarter of the lights in this country still had keepers. The last staffed lighthouse here was automated in 1998. Today, satellite navigation has reduced our dependence on lighthouses, but many are preserved as heritage sites.

items.vi: Giảng viên nói hoàn thành khoảng năm 280 trước Công nguyên.

Estimates of its height vary, but most historians believe it was about one hundred meters tall, which made it one of the tallest structures in the world for many centuries. At night a fire burned at the top, and its light may have been reflected out to sea by sheets of polished bronze.

After the fall of the Roman Empire, many coastal lights went out. In medieval Europe, the few that survived were often kept by monks, who lit beacons on cliffs and headlands as an act of charity for sailors. The fuel was usually wood, and later coal, which burned for longer but produced a great deal of smoke that blackened the glass of the lantern.

Real progress came in the eighteenth century. Early towers built on rocks in the open sea were repeatedly destroyed by storms. In 1750 an engineer named Walter Greaves built the Grayrock Lighthouse using blocks of granite cut so that they locked into each other like the pieces of a puzzle. The blocks were joined with what are known as dovetail joints, and the tower stood for over a hundred years.

The next breakthrough was optical. In the 1820s, a French physicist designed a lens made of concentric rings of glass prisms. It could bend the light from a small lamp into a powerful beam, and it was far lighter than the solid lenses that had been tried before. Light from these lenses could be seen from more than thirty kilometers away.

A lighthouse keeper's life was hard. Keepers took turns to watch the light all night, and they had to climb the stairs every few hours to wind up the clockwork mechanism that turned the lens. If a keeper forgot, the beam stopped sweeping and ships could no longer recognize the light. In fog, light was no use at all, so many stations also had a foghorn, which replaced the old system of ringing a bell.

During the twentieth century, electricity changed the work. Automatic systems were introduced in the 1960s, but they were installed slowly, and even in 1990 about a quarter of the lights in this country still had keepers. The last staffed lighthouse here was automated in 1998. Today, satellite navigation has reduced our dependence on lighthouses, but many are preserved as heritage sites.

items.text:
A
On a calm summer evening, the temperature in the center of a large city can be five to ten degrees Fahrenheit higher than in the farmland beyond its edge. This difference, known as the urban heat island effect, was first described in the early nineteenth century by an amateur meteorologist who recorded the temperatures of his home city for several years and noticed that it was consistently warmer at night than the surrounding countryside. For two centuries the phenomenon remained a curiosity of weather science. Today, as more than half of the world's population lives in cities, it has become a pressing question of public health and energy policy.

B
Several causes work together. Natural landscapes such as forests and meadows cool the air in two ways. Leaves provide shade, and plants release water vapor through their pores, a process called evapotranspiration, which uses up heat energy in much the same way that sweat cools the skin. Cities replace this living surface with dark, dry materials. Asphalt and roofing tiles absorb most of the sunlight that strikes them and give it back slowly after sunset, which is why urban nights stay warm. Tall buildings add to the problem. They trap heat between their walls, and they slow the wind that might otherwise carry it away. Finally, air conditioners, vehicles and factories release waste heat directly into the streets.

C
The consequences go well beyond discomfort. Hot nights are particularly dangerous because the human body needs a period of cooler temperatures in order to recover from the strain of the day. During heat waves, hospital admissions and deaths rise faster in dense neighborhoods than in leafy suburbs, and elderly people who live alone on the upper floors of buildings are at greatest risk. High temperatures also push up electricity demand, as households switch on air conditioning, and the extra waste heat that this releases outdoors makes the street hotter still, creating a feedback loop. In addition, heat speeds up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, so the hottest air in a city is often also its most polluted.

D
Planners have tested a range of remedies. The most familiar is planting trees. A study of the northern city of Halvorsen found that streets where the canopy covered at least 40 percent of the sky were, on average, three degrees cooler on summer afternoons than comparable streets with little cover. Trees, however, need water, space and years to mature, and they cannot be planted on every rooftop. Green roofs, which are covered with soil and plants, offer an alternative. Besides cooling the building beneath, they absorb rainwater and so reduce flooding. Their weight and maintenance needs, though, make them costly to install on older buildings that were not designed to carry them.

E
A cheaper approach is to change the color of surfaces. So-called cool roofs are coated with pale, reflective paint or membranes that bounce much of the sunlight back into the sky. In trials in the port city of Marrow Bay, top-floor apartments under reflective roofs were up to four degrees cooler indoors than those under dark roofs, and their owners spent less on electricity in summer. Critics point out, however, that reflective surfaces at street level can direct heat onto pedestrians, and that in cold climates a reflective roof may raise winter heating bills because it also reflects the weak winter sun. For this reason, most experts advise choosing measures to suit the local climate instead of applying a single solution everywhere.

F
The layout of a city matters as much as its surfaces. Narrow, winding streets cast shade, whereas wide, straight avenues that run in the direction of the prevailing wind can act as channels that flush hot air out. Some cities have therefore protected ventilation corridors, strips of low buildings and parks that bring cooler air from the outskirts into the center. Water features such as fountains and ponds also help, but less than people expect, because their cooling effect rarely extends more than a few dozen meters.

G
Measuring the problem is a challenge in itself. Official weather stations are usually located in open parks or at airports, which can give a misleading picture of conditions in crowded streets. To fill the gap, researchers have begun to use satellites carrying thermal cameras, together with low-cost sensors fixed to buses, bicycles and lamp posts. The maps that result often reveal an uncomfortable pattern: the hottest districts are frequently the poorest, because they have fewer trees and parks and more paved land. Heat has therefore become an issue of fairness as well as of engineering. Some city councils now require developers to submit a heat assessment with their building plans, in the same way that they already submit assessments of traffic and flood risk.
