items.text:
A
Ask most people where money came from and they will describe barter. In a time before coins, the story goes, a farmer who needed shoes traded wheat to a shoemaker, and over the centuries the clumsiness of such swaps drove people to invent money. The tale is neat, and it has been repeated in textbooks since the eighteenth century. Yet anthropologists who have studied small-scale societies around the world have never found a community that ran mainly on barter. What they have found instead are webs of credit and obligation. Neighbors give help or food and remember who owes what, and accounts are settled at festivals, weddings or harvests. Strangers, not neighbors, are the people most likely to trade goods directly for goods.

B
Credit, rather than coinage, may therefore be the older invention. Clay tablets from the temples of southern Mesopotamia, dating from about 3000 BCE, record quantities of barley and silver owed by farmers to temple administrators. Barley was measured in a standard unit, and silver served as a unit of account: prices were written down as weights of silver even when payment was made in grain. The records show that money as a way of measuring value existed long before money as a physical object passed from hand to hand. Debts could be written, transferred and canceled without a single coin changing hands.

C
Physical money took many forms. Cowrie shells, collected from warm seas, circulated across Africa, South Asia and China for thousands of years. They were small, durable and difficult to imitate, which are exactly the qualities a good token needs. In other regions people used salt, cattle, beads and woven cloth. On the Pacific island of Yap, huge limestone wheels, some taller than a person, were used for major transactions. Because the stones were too heavy to move, ownership could change without the stone going anywhere; the community simply remembered who now owned it. In effect, the islanders had created a public ledger, something close to a modern bank account.

D
Metal coins appeared in the kingdom of Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, around 600 BCE. The earliest Lydian coins were made of electrum, a natural mixture of gold and silver, and were stamped with a mark guaranteeing their weight and purity. The stamp was the real innovation. Before it, a merchant had to weigh and test metal at every transaction. A trusted stamp from the ruler allowed coins to be counted instead of weighed. Rulers soon saw further advantages. Coins carrying a royal emblem advertised the ruler's authority, and they could be used to pay soldiers, who would spend them in local markets, spreading the coins and the ruler's image through the economy. Governments also discovered that they could cheat by reducing the precious metal in each coin, a practice known as debasement. It has recurred throughout history and usually leads to rising prices.

E
Paper money first appeared in China. By the eleventh century, merchants had begun to leave heavy strings of copper coins with trusted deposit shops and to receive paper receipts, which could be exchanged for goods like cash. The government later took over the system and issued official notes. European travelers in the thirteenth century were astonished that mere paper could be accepted as payment. Yet the Chinese experience also supplied the first warning: when emperors printed too many notes to pay for wars, the notes lost value. In Europe, paper money developed from the receipts that goldsmiths gave to customers who stored gold with them. The goldsmiths noticed that depositors never came to collect their gold all at once, and so they began to lend out part of it, which was the beginning of modern banking.

F
Today, most money exists only as numbers on computer screens, and notes and coins make up a small share of the money supply in most developed countries. Some economists see this as a return to the oldest form of money, a record of who owes what. Whether new digital currencies will become true money remains to be seen. Economists generally agree that money must fill three roles: a medium of exchange, a store of value and a unit of account. Many digital tokens can be used for payment, but their wildly changing prices make them poor at the second role, since few people want to keep savings in something that may lose half its value in a month. History suggests that what makes money is not the material but the trust people place in it.

Deposit shops were safer than governments.
Foreign merchants refused to accept paper.
Printing too many notes could make them lose their value.

wanted to stop customers from collecting their gold

options: They have already replaced notes and coins.
They cannot be used for payment.
They are trusted more than government money.
Their unstable prices weaken their role as a store of value.
items.vi: Đoạn F: giá biến động mạnh khiến chúng kém trong vai trò lưu trữ giá trị.

items.text:
A
Each autumn, a bar-tailed godwit leaves Alaska and flies roughly 11,000 kilometers to New Zealand without stopping to eat, drink or rest, a journey that lasts about eight days. Arctic terns travel from the far north to the Antarctic and back again, a round trip that can exceed 70,000 kilometers. Sea turtles cross entire oceans and return to lay their eggs on the beaches where they hatched decades earlier. Such feats raise an obvious question: how do animals find their way with no maps, no compasses and no one to ask? Over the past century, researchers have discovered that there is no single answer. Instead, animals appear to carry a toolkit of senses, each suited to different conditions.

B
The simplest tool is memory. Many animals learn the features of their home area and use them as landmarks, and some species have remarkable spatial memories. A Clark's nutcracker, a bird of mountain forests, may hide tens of thousands of pine seeds in thousands of separate places in a single autumn, and recover most of them months later, often when they are buried under snow. Experiments suggest that the birds do not search at random but remember the position of each store in relation to rocks, trees and other objects. Yet memory alone cannot explain a journey across open ocean, where there are no landmarks at all.

C
For long journeys, many animals look to the sky. Honeybees use the sun as a compass. When a forager returns to the hive, she performs a waggle dance in which the angle of her body relative to vertical shows the angle of the food source relative to the sun. Because the sun moves across the sky, bees and birds must also consult an internal clock to correct for the time of day. Night migrants rely on stars. In a classic experiment, young indigo buntings were raised in a planetarium in which the sky was made to turn around a different star from the real one. When they were old enough to migrate, they took their bearings from the point around which they had seen the sky rotate, showing that they had learned the pattern of stars during their first weeks of life rather than inheriting a map of it.
D
Clouds and darkness do not stop migration, and this led scientists to look for a sense that works in any weather: the detection of the Earth's magnetic field. Robins kept in cages in autumn hop restlessly in the direction in which they would fly, even when they cannot see the sky, and they change direction when the magnetic field around them is altered. Two explanations have been proposed. According to the first, tiny crystals of magnetite, a magnetic mineral, in the head or beak act like compass needles. According to the second, light-sensitive proteins in the eye react to the field and allow the bird, in effect, to see it as a pattern laid over its normal view. Support for the second idea came when robins exposed to weak radio-frequency noise lost their sense of direction, since such noise would disturb a chemical reaction in the proteins but would have no effect on a crystal. Neither theory has been conclusively proved, and both may be partly right. Sea turtles use the field too. Hatchlings seem to learn the magnetic signature of their home beach, a particular combination of field strength and angle, and use it years later to find their way back.

E
Smell is another important sense. Pigeons deprived of their sense of smell often fail to find their way home when they are released in unfamiliar places. In one experiment, seabirds called shearwaters were treated so that they could not detect odors and were taken to a distant release site. Untreated birds flew home, but many of the treated birds either did not return or took much longer. Salmon provide the best-known example. Young fish memorize the chemical signature of their home stream, and years later, after living at sea, they find it again by following the scent upstream, even though they may have traveled thousands of kilometers.

F
Not all navigation requires outside cues. Desert ants of the genus Cataglyphis forage on featureless salt flats, wandering in winding paths for up to a hundred meters from the nest, yet when they find food they return in a straight line. They achieve this by path integration, continually adding up each turn they make and the distance they travel. How do they measure distance? In an ingenious experiment, researchers glued tiny stilts made of pig bristle to the legs of some ants and trimmed the legs of others to stumps. Ants on stilts, taking longer strides, walked past the nest before they began to search, while those with stumps stopped short of it. The result suggests that the ants count their steps.

G
Because animals combine cues, the failure of one rarely leaves them lost. A bird under cloud may switch from the stars to the magnetic field, and a pigeon over unfamiliar land may use smell and then, nearer home, landmarks. Yet human activity is interfering with these systems. Artificial lights near beaches draw hatchling turtles toward roads instead of the sea, and bright city lights confuse night-migrating birds, which circle buildings until they are exhausted. Studying animal navigation therefore has a practical side for conservation, and engineers are interested in it too. Robots that rely on ant-like path integration could move in places that satellite signals do not reach, such as tunnels or underwater.

items.text:
The table shows the percentage of commuters in the city of Brightmoor who used five different ways of travelling to work in 2000, 2010 and 2020.

Car: 62 (2000), 55 (2010), 44 (2020)
Bus: 18 (2000), 17 (2010), 12 (2020)
Train: 9 (2000), 14 (2010), 18 (2020)
Bicycle: 3 (2000), 6 (2010), 14 (2020)
Walking: 8 (2000), 8 (2010), 12 (2020)
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table shows the percentage of commuters in Brightmoor who used five different ways of travelling to work in 2000, 2010 and 2020. Overall, car use fell significantly over the period, while cycling and walking became much more popular.

In 2000, the car was by far the most common choice, used by 62 percent of commuters, followed by the bus at 18 percent. Train travel accounted for 9 percent and walking for 8 percent, and only 3 percent of people cycled.

By 2010, the share of car commuters had dropped to 55 percent, and the proportion using the train had risen to 14 percent. Cycling doubled to 6 percent, whereas bus use and walking remained almost unchanged at 17 and 8 percent respectively.

The trend continued in 2020. Car use declined further to 44 percent, a fall of 18 percentage points since 2000. The most dramatic change was in cycling, which rose from 3 percent to 14 percent and overtook the bus, which fell to 12 percent. Train use grew steadily to 18 percent, and walking rose to 12 percent.

parts.instr: You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.

items.q: Some people think that schools should spend more time teaching practical life skills, such as cooking, managing money and basic repairs, instead of traditional academic subjects. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
items.sample:
Practical skills such as cooking, budgeting and basic repairs are useful in everyday life, yet they are rarely taught in a systematic way. Some people argue that schools should give them more time than traditional academic subjects. I agree that these skills deserve a place in the curriculum, but I do not think they should replace academic study.

The main argument in favor of practical lessons is that many young adults leave school unprepared for independent life. A graduate may be able to solve an equation but not know how to compare the interest rates on a loan, or how to cook a healthy meal on a small budget. As a result, they may fall into debt or rely on cheap fast food. Short, well-designed courses on money management and nutrition could prevent these problems and would benefit society as a whole. Practical lessons can also motivate students who find traditional classes dull, because the results are visible and immediately useful.

However, reducing academic subjects would be a mistake. Mathematics, science and languages develop reasoning and communication skills that are needed in almost every career, and they open the door to university study. Moreover, many practical skills are really applications of academic knowledge. Cooking involves measurement and chemistry, while budgeting is simple arithmetic. A student with a strong academic base can learn these skills quickly, whereas the opposite is not always true. In addition, families and communities can teach many practical skills at home, but few parents can teach advanced physics or a foreign language.

In conclusion, schools should add practical lessons to the timetable, perhaps for one or two hours each week, because they prepare students for real life. Nevertheless, academic subjects should remain the core of education, since they provide the foundation on which all other learning is built.
items.vi: Bài mẫu đồng ý một phần: kỹ năng thực hành cần có trong chương trình nhưng không thay thế môn học thuật. Cấu trúc: mở bài nêu quan điểm, một đoạn ủng hộ, một đoạn phản biện, kết luận.

items.vi: Trả lời có/không về việc nấu ăn và đưa lý do.

items.q: What do you usually do at the weekend?
items.sample: At the weekend I usually sleep a little later, and then I do my homework. In the afternoon I often meet my friends to play football or just to talk at a cafe.
items.vi: Miêu tả hoạt động thường làm cuối tuần, dùng trạng từ tần suất.

parts.instr: Part 2: Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2: nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a skill that you learned from another person. You should say: what the skill is, who taught you, how you learned it, and explain why it has been useful to you.
items.sample:
I would like to talk about a skill that I learned from my uncle, which is how to repair bicycles. My uncle owns a small workshop near our house, and he has been fixing bikes for more than twenty years. When I was thirteen, my own bike broke down, and instead of buying a new one, he suggested that I learn to repair it myself.

He taught me step by step. First he showed me the names of the parts, such as the chain, the brakes and the gears. Then he let me take the wheel off and fix a flat tire while he watched. I made many mistakes at the beginning, and my hands were always covered in oil, but he was very patient and he never took the tools from me. I learned mainly by doing the work again and again during my school holidays.

This skill has been useful to me in several ways. Firstly, I save money, because I can repair my friends' bikes as well as my own. Secondly, it taught me to be patient and to solve problems carefully. Finally, it gave me a special bond with my uncle, and I will always be grateful to him for teaching me.
items.vi: Bài mẫu kể về kỹ năng sửa xe đạp học từ chú: nêu kỹ năng, người dạy, cách học và lợi ích. Dùng thì quá khứ cho câu chuyện và hiện tại hoàn thành cho lợi ích đến nay.

parts.instr: Part 3: Discuss more abstract questions related to the Part 2 topic.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3: thảo luận các câu hỏi trừu tượng liên quan đến chủ đề phần 2.

items.q: Why do some people find it easier to learn new skills than others?
items.sample: I think there are several reasons. Some people are naturally more curious, so they are more motivated to practice, and practice is the most important factor. Others had good teachers or supportive families when they were young. Also, people who are afraid of making mistakes often learn more slowly, because they avoid trying new things.
items.vi: Nêu vài nguyên nhân: động lực, luyện tập, người dạy và nỗi sợ mắc lỗi.

items.q: Do you think schools or families should be responsible for teaching practical skills?
items.sample: I think both should share the responsibility. Families are the best place to teach everyday habits such as cooking or cleaning, because children can learn by watching their parents. However, schools can make sure that every student learns the basics, including those whose parents are too busy, so schools and families should work together.
items.vi: Trình bày quan điểm: cả gia đình và nhà trường cùng chịu trách nhiệm, có lý do cho mỗi bên.

items.q: How might technology change the way people learn skills in the future?
items.sample: In the future, I think technology will make it easier to learn almost any skill. People will use virtual reality to practice difficult tasks safely, and online videos and apps will give them personal feedback. However, I believe that real practice with a human teacher will still be important, because a teacher can notice small mistakes that a program might miss.
items.vi: Dự đoán tác động của công nghệ (thực tế ảo, video, ứng dụng) và nêu giới hạn so với giáo viên thật.

audio.t: Good morning, Riverside Arts Centre. How can I help you?
Hello. I would like to book a place on your pottery course for adults, please.
Certainly. Could I have your surname?
It's Brennan. That's B-R-E-N-N-A-N.
Thank you, Mr. Brennan. And a contact number?
Let me read that back: 07700 482913. Good. Now, there are two groups. The Wednesday group is full, but we have places in the Thursday evening group.
Thursday is fine. What time does it start?
Half past six, but that was last year. No, sorry, I'm looking at the old leaflet. The class begins at seven p.m. and finishes at nine.
Seven, great. And how long does the course last? I saw twelve weeks on the website.
That was the old course. The new one is shorter. It runs for eight weeks.
And what is the fee?
It's one hundred and twenty dollars normally, but there is a discount for people who book before the end of the month, so you pay ninety-six dollars.
That's very good. What does that include?
All the clay, and also the glazes for painting your pots. You don't need to buy anything extra, but it is a good idea to bring an old apron, because the work gets messy.
I'll bring one. Where exactly do the classes take place?
In Studio C, on the first floor. If you park in the car park behind the library, you can walk to the centre in two minutes. The car park at the front is always full in the evening.
Thanks very much. I'm looking forward to it.

audio.t: Good evening and welcome to Local Matters. Tonight we look at the Millbrook Bike Library, which opened in the spring of 2021. The idea was first discussed in 2019, but it took two years to find the money and the space.

Many people assume the library was created to help hospital staff, because a group of nurses did complain at the time that buses to the hospital were too infrequent. In fact the council's main aim was different. It wanted to cut the number of cars in the town center, which had become badly congested on market days.

The scheme began with only forty bikes, kept at three stations. Today there are one hundred and twenty bikes at eleven stations. Some residents say the number should be two hundred, but the manager, Ms. Ortega, says that would be too many for the available space.

Using the library is simple. You do not need a monthly card or a phone app. You leave a deposit of ten dollars, which is returned when you bring the bike back. You can keep a bike for up to twenty-four hours.

Who uses the bikes? You might expect students, and they do use them, but the largest group is actually retired people, who say the bikes give them independence for shopping and visiting friends. Office workers come next, and families use them mainly at weekends.

The scheme has had problems. Vandalism was expected, but in fact it has been rare. The real difficulty is that people leave bikes far from the stations, so that popular stations are empty while others have too many bikes. Staff spend several hours each day driving around to move them.

To solve this, the library introduced a system of credits last year. If you return a bike to a station that is nearly empty, you earn credits that give you free ride time. Fines were considered, but the manager felt they would put people off using the scheme, and tracking devices on every bike were simply too expensive.

On the question of money, the library does not make a profit. About half of the running costs are covered by a national transport grant, and the council pays most of the rest. Sponsors give a little, and users' deposits are never spent, so they are not counted as income.

Looking ahead, the biggest plan is to introduce electric bikes, which would help people in the hilly northern part of town. Extending the service to the villages was discussed, but that has been postponed until next year at least.

If you want to suggest a place for a new station, you can phone the library helpline, which is open from nine until five on weekdays. You can also write to the council, but the staff say that the phone is the quickest way. That's all for tonight. Thanks for listening.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your field project proposal?
Yes, Dr. Ellis. We would like to study whether rooftop beehives improve fruit production in nearby community gardens.
Interesting. How did you come up with the idea?
Well, Mina wanted to do something about bees after reading an article about falling insect numbers, and I suggested the rooftops, because my cousin keeps hives on a hospital roof.
Right. At first I had planned to survey gardeners about what they plant, but Tom pointed out that wouldn't tell us anything about the bees themselves.
He's right. So how will you measure pollination?
We thought of counting the fruit on tomato plants in six gardens, three within a kilometer of the hives and three further away.
That's a reasonable start, but tomatoes are partly self-pollinating, so bees may make less difference than you expect. Squash would give a clearer result.
Squash, then. They need insects to carry the pollen. But we would have to persuade the gardeners to grow them.
Many will agree if you offer them free seeds.
That's a good idea. What about the timing? The hives are active from April to September, and our report is due in October.
Then July and August would be best, when the plants are flowering. Though many students leave for the summer.
I'll be here. Mina is traveling in August, so she'll do the analysis when she gets back.
Fine. One concern is the number of variables. Weather, soil and wild bees will all affect the results. How will you deal with that?
We'll record the weather every day and note any wild bees we see. Tom also thinks we should include one garden far from any hives as a control.
Yes, a control is essential. But recording every wild bee will take too much time. Just do ten-minute counts, twice a week.
That's much more realistic. And what about permission? Do we need it from the roof owners?
You need written permission from the building manager, and the hives must be checked by a licensed beekeeper. Do you have one?
My uncle is licensed, and he said he would inspect them every two weeks.

Excellent. Please submit the permission form by Friday. One last piece of advice. Start writing the methods section now, before you collect any data. Everyone leaves it until the end and then forgets the details.
We'll do that. Thank you, Dr. Ellis.

audio.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at tidal energy, one of the most predictable sources of renewable power.

Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the moon, with a smaller contribution from the sun. As the Earth turns, most coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides each day, so the energy is available twice every cycle, and engineers can forecast it years ahead. That is a big advantage over wind or solar power.

However, tidal energy only works well in places where the difference between high and low water, the tidal range, is large. As a rule, a range of at least five meters is needed, and few coastlines have that.

There are two main technologies. The older one is the barrage, which is a kind of dam built across a bay or river mouth. Water flows in as the tide rises, and flows out through turbines as it falls. The first large barrage was completed in the 1960s and it is still working today.

The newer technology is the tidal stream turbine. These look like underwater windmills and they are fixed to the seabed, where fast currents turn the blades. Because water is about eight hundred times denser than air, the blades can be smaller than a wind turbine's and they turn slowly, which is better for sea life.

Environmental effects are the main concern with barrages. They can block the movement of fish, and they change the way sediment is carried, so that mud builds up in some places and disappears in others. Turbines have much less effect, though researchers are still studying whether seals and diving birds can be injured.

The biggest obstacle is cost. Building a barrage is extremely expensive, and the electricity it produces costs more than from many other sources. On the other hand, the machines last a very long time. A well-built barrage can operate for around one hundred twenty years, compared with about twenty-five for a wind farm.
To sum up, tidal power is reliable but limited by geography and money. Our next session will look at wave energy, which has different problems. Please read the first chapter before then.

The biggest obstacle is cost. Building a barrage is extremely expensive, and the electricity it produces costs more than from many other sources. On the other hand, the machines last a very long time. A well-built barrage can operate for around one hundred twenty years, compared with about twenty-five for a wind farm.
To sum up, tidal power is reliable but limited by geography and money. Our next session will look at wave energy, which has different problems. Please read the first chapter before then.

audio.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at tidal energy, one of the most predictable sources of renewable power.

Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the moon, with a smaller contribution from the sun. As the Earth turns, most coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides each day, so the energy is available twice every cycle, and engineers can forecast it years ahead. That is a big advantage over wind or solar power.

However, tidal energy only works well in places where the difference between high and low water, the tidal range, is large. As a rule, a range of at least five meters is needed, and few coastlines have that.

There are two main technologies. The older one is the barrage, which is a kind of dam built across a bay or river mouth. Water flows in as the tide rises, and flows out through turbines as it falls. The first large barrage was completed in the 1960s and it is still working today.

The newer technology is the tidal stream turbine. These look like underwater windmills and they are fixed to the seabed, where fast currents turn the blades. Because water is about eight hundred times denser than air, the blades can be smaller than a wind turbine's and they turn slowly, which is better for sea life.

Environmental effects are the main concern with barrages. They can block the movement of fish, and they change the way sediment is carried, so that mud builds up in some places and disappears in others. Turbines have much less effect, though researchers are still studying whether seals and diving birds can be injured.

The biggest obstacle is cost. Building a barrage is extremely expensive, and the electricity it produces costs more than from many other sources. On the other hand, the machines last a very long time. A well-built barrage can operate for around one hundred twenty years, compared with about twenty-five for a wind farm.
To sum up, tidal power is reliable but limited by geography and money. Our next session will look at wave energy, which has different problems. Please read the first chapter before then.

items.text:
The Placebo Effect: Medicine in the Mind

A. For most of the twentieth century, the placebo was regarded as little more than a nuisance. A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill or an injection of salt water, and its traditional role was to act as a baseline in clinical trials. If patients taking a new drug improved more than those taking the placebo, the drug was judged to work. Yet researchers kept noticing something awkward: patients in the placebo group often got better too, sometimes dramatically. This improvement became known as the placebo effect, and for decades it was treated as statistical noise to be subtracted from the results rather than a phenomenon worth studying in its own right.

B. Interest changed when scientists began to ask what happens inside the body of a patient who receives a placebo. Brain imaging studies of people with chronic pain showed that an inert pill can trigger the release of endorphins, the body's natural painkillers. When the same patients were given a drug that blocks endorphins, the pain relief from the placebo disappeared. This result suggested that the effect was not imaginary. Expectation, it seemed, could set off real chemical changes. Later work on Parkinson's disease found that patients who believed they had received an effective drug showed a surge of dopamine in the brain, even though the injection contained only salt water.

C. The strength of a placebo depends on surprisingly small details. In one series of experiments, volunteers with tension headaches were given identical white tablets. Those told that the tablets were a well-known pain reliever reported greater relief than those told only that the tablets were "a medicine", although every tablet was the same sugar pill. Color also seems to matter: red and orange pills are generally judged more stimulating, while blue and green ones are linked with calm. Two pills are often more powerful than one, an injection more powerful than a tablet, and an expensive product more powerful than a cheap one. Such patterns do not mean that patients are foolish. They suggest that the brain constantly builds predictions about the future from past experience, and that these predictions influence what we actually feel.

D. The effect is also shaped by the person who delivers the treatment. In a study of patients with irritable bowel syndrome, participants were divided into three groups. One group was placed on a waiting list and received nothing, so that the researchers could see how symptoms changed with no treatment at all. A second group received sham acupuncture from a practitioner who spoke little and avoided eye contact. A third group received the same sham treatment from a practitioner who was warm, asked questions, and expressed confidence that the treatment would help. After three weeks, the third group reported by far the greatest improvement. The researchers concluded that the relationship between patient and caregiver was itself a powerful part of the therapy, and that it could be delivered at no extra cost.

E. One of the most surprising discoveries is that a placebo can work even when patients know exactly what it is. In an "open-label" trial, volunteers with long-term back pain were given pills clearly labeled "placebo" and were told honestly that they contained no medicine. The researchers explained that the body can respond automatically to the ritual of taking a pill, and asked the volunteers to take it twice daily anyway. Over three weeks, these patients reported less pain and less disability than a comparison group who received no pills. The study was small, and larger trials will be needed, but it challenges the assumption that deception is necessary for the effect to occur.

F. Not every condition responds equally. Placebos appear to influence symptoms that are experienced subjectively, such as pain, nausea, fatigue and low mood, but there is no good evidence that they can shrink a tumor or cure an infection. This limit raises an ethical problem. Doctors who prescribe placebos in place of proven treatments risk harming patients, and they may damage trust if the truth emerges. Many specialists therefore argue that the lesson of the placebo effect is not to hand out sugar pills but to improve ordinary medicine: to explain treatments clearly, to listen to patients, and to set realistic and hopeful expectations. In this view, the placebo effect is not the opposite of real medicine. It is a part of it that has always been present and is only now being understood.

items.text:
Glacier Retreat and the Rising Sea

A. Glaciers are slow rivers of ice. They form where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer, and over centuries the accumulated snow is compressed into dense ice that begins to flow downhill under its own weight. Around the world there are roughly 200,000 glaciers, from small patches clinging to mountain slopes to great tongues of ice that reach the sea. Together with the two vast ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, they hold about two thirds of the planet's fresh water. Because this ice is so sensitive to temperature, glaciers are often described as the thermometers of the mountains.

B. Scientists describe the health of a glacier by its mass balance, the difference between the snow it gains each year and the ice it loses through melting and other processes. A glacier with a positive balance grows, and one with a negative balance shrinks. Since the 1980s, the large majority of mountain glaciers have had a negative balance in most years. The Tarnfjell Glacier in a northern range, for instance, has retreated by about 2.4 kilometers since 1950, leaving behind bare rock and a cold gray lake where thick ice once lay. Its fate in the future depends on temperatures that nobody can predict exactly, and researchers are wary of giving a date for its disappearance.

C. The link between glaciers and sea level is often misunderstood. Melting sea ice makes almost no difference to the height of the ocean, because floating ice already displaces its own weight of water, in the same way that an ice cube melting in a glass leaves the water level unchanged. What matters is ice that rests on land. When it melts, the water flows into the sea and adds to its volume. A second cause is thermal expansion: as the ocean warms, the water itself takes up more space. Over the last century, these two effects have together raised the global average sea level by more than twenty centimeters. If every mountain glacier melted, the sea would rise by only about 0.3 meters, but the ice sheets are a very different matter. Greenland holds enough ice to raise the sea by about seven meters, and Antarctica enough for roughly fifty-eight.

D. The way ice sheets lose mass is more complicated than simple melting. Much of their ice flows toward the coast in fast-moving streams, and at the edge it either breaks off into the ocean as icebergs, a process called calving, or spreads out over the water as floating shelves. These shelves act like a cork, holding back the ice behind them. When warm ocean water melts the shelves from below, or when they crack and break apart, the ice behind can speed up and discharge into the sea much more quickly. Some scientists fear that parts of Antarctica, where the bed lies far below sea level, may be vulnerable to a self-reinforcing retreat that is difficult to stop once it has begun.

E. Sea level does not rise evenly across the globe. A huge ice sheet pulls the ocean toward it with its gravity, so that sea level near Greenland is higher than it would otherwise be. When the sheet shrinks, that pull weakens, and water moves away. The result is that sea level close to a melting ice sheet can actually fall, while far-off coasts experience a larger rise than the global average. The land itself is also changing. Freed from the enormous weight of ice, the crust beneath former glaciers slowly rises, in some parts of Scandinavia by almost a centimeter a year. For a city planner, therefore, a global figure is of limited use, and local measurements are essential.

F. Glaciers matter to people long before the sea level rises. In many mountain regions they act as natural reservoirs, storing water as snow and ice in winter and releasing it in the warm, dry months when rivers are low. As glaciers shrink, the flow of meltwater first increases and then declines, and the point at which the flow is at its highest is known as peak water. Communities that depend on glacial rivers for farming, drinking water and hydropower must prepare for the time after this peak. Retreating ice also creates new hazards. Lakes forming behind loose piles of rock can burst suddenly and send floods racing down valleys, endangering villages far below.

G. Measuring these changes has become easier. Satellites now track the thickness of ice sheets with laser instruments, and they can detect tiny shifts in the planet's gravity caused by ice loss. Even so, the uncertainties remain large. Some ice has already been committed to melting because of the warming that has taken place, and the speed at which the ice sheets respond will probably decide whether this century's sea level rise is measured in tens of centimeters or in meters. What is clear is that the rate depends on future emissions, and that coastal communities will need to adapt whichever path the world takes.

items.text:
The Economics of the Music Industry

A. At the end of the 1990s, the recorded music business sold its product mainly in the form of physical discs, and it enjoyed record profits. Within fifteen years, revenue had fallen by nearly half. The cause was not a loss of interest in music, which people consumed more than ever, but a change in the way it could be copied and shared. Digital files could be duplicated perfectly at almost no cost, and in the early years of the internet many listeners saw little reason to pay. Only when streaming services offered a convenient and legal alternative did the industry's income begin to recover.

B. The underlying problem is one that economists have long recognized. Music has a marginal cost close to zero: once a song has been recorded, supplying one more copy costs next to nothing. Goods of this kind are hard to sell at a fair price, because a competitor, or a pirate, can offer the same thing for free. Streaming addressed the problem by changing what is sold. Instead of purchasing copies, listeners pay a monthly subscription for access to a vast catalog. They no longer own anything, but for a small, regular fee they can listen to almost anything they want, and for many people that is a better bargain than buying albums.

C. How the subscription income should be divided is now one of the most argued questions in the business. Under the most common system, all the money is gathered into a single pool, and each artist receives a share equal to their proportion of total streams. A listener who plays a few favorite songs a few times a month therefore contributes very little to those artists, because most of their payment is spread among the most popular acts. Critics favor an alternative, sometimes called the user-centric model, in which a subscriber's fee is divided only among the artists that person actually played. Supporters say this is fairer, but it would shift money from the biggest stars to smaller ones, and it would be more complicated to run, so it has been adopted only in small experiments. In both systems, the payment for a single stream is a fraction of a cent, and an artist's final share is smaller still once the label, distributor and publisher have taken their parts.

D. The digital catalog is enormous, yet the attention of listeners is very unevenly spread. A small number of artists account for a large proportion of all streams, a pattern that economists call superstar economics. At the same time, the internet makes it possible for niche artists to reach fans in distant countries, and the combined audience of these minor acts can be large even though each one is small. This is known as the long tail. The long tail brings variety for listeners, but it does not guarantee a living for musicians. A typical artist earns a very modest amount from streaming, and many need other jobs to survive.

E. As income from recordings became less dependable, live performance took on a greater role. For many musicians, touring is now the main source of income, and recordings serve partly as advertisements for the concerts. Demand has pushed ticket prices up, and some promoters adjust them according to demand, in the way that airlines do. However, the costs of travel, crew, equipment and venue hire are considerable, and for emerging artists a tour often loses money. The pandemic years showed how fragile this arrangement can be, because the loss of live events took away income that recordings alone could not replace.

F. The role of intermediaries has also changed. Record labels once controlled the only route to a national audience, but today an artist can use a distribution service to place music on every major platform without signing to anyone. Such artists keep a larger share of the revenue, but they must pay for recording, promotion and legal advice themselves, and they carry the entire risk of failure. Labels still offer something that many musicians value: money in advance, expertise in marketing, and the ability to push a song to the attention of millions. Songwriters, meanwhile, earn income from separate rights, including payments when their work appears in films and advertisements, which can be worth more than streaming.

G. What will happen next is hard to say. Music now competes for time with video, games and social media, and the total amount of attention is limited. Some economists expect revenue to remain concentrated in the hands of a few large companies and stars, while others point to growing platforms where fans fund their favorite artists directly. It seems unlikely that one model will suit every musician. The industry is probably heading toward a mixture of arrangements, in which the balance between streaming, live shows and direct support will differ from one artist to another, and in which success will remain unpredictable.

items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares how many hours adults spent each week listening to music through five different formats over a thirty-year period. Overall, streaming grew from nothing to become the most popular format, while physical discs and radio declined steadily.

In 1995, radio was the main way of listening, at nine hours a week, followed by physical discs at seven hours. Neither downloads nor streaming existed in the figures, and live concerts accounted for only half an hour. By 2005, radio and discs had fallen slightly to eight and six hours, and downloads appeared at two hours.

The biggest change came after 2005. Streaming rose from zero to five hours in 2015 and then almost tripled to 14 hours in 2025, the highest figure in the whole table. In contrast, physical discs dropped to just one hour by 2025, and radio fell to four hours. Downloads increased to three hours in 2015 but then fell back to one hour as listeners moved to streaming.

Live concerts remained small and stable, rising only slightly from 0.5 to 0.7 hours. This suggests that, although the way people listen at home has changed dramatically, attending live music has stayed a minor but steady habit.
items.vi: Mô tả xu hướng chính: streaming tăng mạnh nhất (0 lên 14 giờ), đĩa và radio giảm, hòa nhạc trực tiếp ổn định. Dùng từ so sánh và số liệu, không nêu ý kiến cá nhân.

parts.instr: Writing Task 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write at least 250 words.
parts.instrVi: Bài viết 2. Dành khoảng 40 phút. Viết ít nhất 250 từ.

items.q: Some people believe that museums should be free for everyone, while others think visitors should pay an entrance fee. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
items.sample:
Museums are important places where people can learn about history, science and art. Some people argue that they should be free, while others believe visitors should pay. In my opinion, free entry is the better policy, although it needs careful funding.

Those who support entrance fees make a reasonable point. Museums are expensive to run, because they must pay for security, conservation, staff and new exhibitions. If visitors contribute, the museum becomes less dependent on government money, and it may be able to protect its collections better. Some people also argue that a small fee makes visitors value the experience more, so they spend more time looking carefully.

However, I believe the advantages of free entry are greater. First, museums exist for the benefit of the whole of society, and a fee can stop families on low incomes from visiting. A child who never enters a museum may never discover an interest in science or history. Second, free museums usually attract many more visitors. When one city made its main museum free, attendance doubled, and many of the new visitors were young people who had never visited before. These visitors also spend money in the museum shop and the cafe, which helps to cover some of the costs.

To solve the problem of funding, governments could pay for basic entrance, while museums charge for special exhibitions or accept voluntary donations. This way, everyone can enter, but those who can afford more can still support the museum.

In conclusion, although fees can raise money, I think that free access serves the public better, provided that there are other sources of income to keep museums working well.
items.vi: Bài thảo luận hai quan điểm: nêu lý do cho vé vào cửa và cho miễn phí, rồi đưa ý kiến riêng với ví dụ rõ ràng. Bố cục: mở bài, hai đoạn thân bài, kết bài.

parts.instr: Part 1. Answer the questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1. Trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: Let's talk about your hometown. What do you like most about the place where you live?
items.sample: What I like most about my hometown is the people, because they are friendly and always ready to help. I also like the small parks where I can relax after school.
items.vi: Trả lời về điều bạn thích nhất ở quê hương, nêu lý do bằng because.

items.q: Do you enjoy cooking? Why or why not?
items.sample: Yes, I enjoy cooking, because it is relaxing and I can make something for my family. At weekends I try new recipes, although sometimes I make a mess in the kitchen.
items.vi: Nói bạn có thích nấu ăn không và giải thích lý do.

items.q: How do people usually travel around your town?
items.sample: Most people travel by motorbike or bus in my town. Some students ride a bike, but the traffic is heavy in the morning, so it can be quite stressful.
items.vi: Mô tả phương tiện đi lại phổ biến ở nơi bạn sống.

items.q: What kind of weather do you like best? Why?
items.sample: I like sunny weather best, because I can go outside and meet my friends. When the weather is too hot, though, I prefer to stay at home and read.
items.vi: Nói loại thời tiết bạn thích nhất và lý do.

parts.instr: Part 2. Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2. Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong một đến hai phút.

items.q: Describe a skill that you learned from another person. You should say: who taught you this skill, what the skill was, how you learned it, and explain why this skill has been useful to you.
items.sample: I would like to talk about a skill that my grandfather taught me, which is how to repair bicycles. My grandfather used to work as a mechanic, and when I was about ten years old, I became interested in his tools. One summer, my bike broke down, and instead of buying a new one, he suggested that we fix it together. At first I only watched him, but gradually he let me take off the wheel, clean the chain and change the tire. He was very patient, and he explained every step slowly, so I could understand what each part does. We spent many afternoons in his small garage, and I learned more from those afternoons than from any book. This skill has been useful to me in several ways. First, I can save money, because I do not need to pay a shop to repair my bike. Second, I often help my friends when something goes wrong with their bikes, which makes me feel proud and confident. Most importantly, the skill reminds me of my grandfather and the time we spent together, which is why it is so special to me.
items.vi: Bài nói Part 2: trả lời đủ 4 ý gợi ý (ai dạy, kỹ năng gì, học thế nào, vì sao hữu ích), nói liền mạch khoảng 2 phút, dùng thì quá khứ.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss the questions about learning.
parts.instrVi: Phần 3. Thảo luận các câu hỏi về việc học.

items.q: Do you think children learn better from teachers or from their families?
items.sample: I think both are important, but in different ways. Teachers are trained to explain difficult subjects clearly, so children learn better from them at school. However, family members teach values and daily skills, because children spend so much time at home with them.
items.vi: Câu hỏi thảo luận: so sánh vai trò của giáo viên và gia đình, nêu lý do.

items.q: How has technology changed the way people learn new skills?
items.sample: Technology has made learning much easier and cheaper. Nowadays people can watch videos online and follow a lesson at any time, so they do not have to attend a class. On the other hand, it is harder to stay focused, and technology cannot replace practice with a real person.
items.vi: Nói về ảnh hưởng của công nghệ đến việc học kỹ năng mới, cả mặt tích cực và hạn chế.

items.q: Should adults keep learning throughout their lives? Why?
items.sample: Yes, I believe adults should keep learning, because the world changes quickly and new jobs need new skills. Learning also keeps the mind active and gives people confidence. Many older adults enjoy courses, which help them make friends and feel useful.
items.vi: Nêu quan điểm về việc học suốt đời và đưa ra lý do cụ thể.

audio.t: Good morning, Lakeside Photography Centre. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to book a place on one of your weekend workshops, please.
Certainly. Can I have your name?
Tomas Hadley.
Could you spell your surname for me?
Yes, it's H-A-D-L-E-Y.
Thank you. Which workshop are you interested in? We have portrait photography, night photography and landscape photography this month.
I think night photography sounds difficult, and I'm not keen on portraits. I'd like the landscape one.
Good choice. It runs on Saturday the seventeenth of October. Sunday is the portrait workshop, so don't get them mixed up.
Saturday the seventeenth, then. What time does it start?
We meet at nine o'clock in the morning. It used to start at eight, but we changed it because of the bus timetable.
That's better for me. How much does it cost?
It's forty-five dollars per person. That includes the guide and a printed photo of your best picture, but lunch is not included.
Is there somewhere to eat nearby?
Yes, there's a small cafe next to the lake, so most people buy something there.
Great. Do I need to bring any special equipment?

Just your camera and a tripod. If you don't have one, we can lend you one, but please tell us in advance. You should also have a memory card with at least sixteen gigabytes of space, because landscape pictures take up a lot of room.
Sixteen gigabytes, no problem. And where do we meet?
Outside the old boathouse, not at the main reception. The boathouse is the white building at the end of the car park.
Thanks. How many people will be in the group?
We keep it small. The maximum is twelve, so you are lucky, there are only two places left.
Then I'll take one. Thank you very much.
You're welcome, Mr. Hadley. We'll send you an email to confirm.

audio.t: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information evening about the new Westbrook Library, which opens its doors next month. I'm Helen Marsh, the project manager, and I'll take about ten minutes to explain what to expect.

First, a little history. The old library on Mill Road served this town for sixty years, but it had become too small and the roof was leaking. The council considered repairing it, but the cost would have been almost as high as building a new one, so it decided to start again on the site of the former bus depot. Building took two years, a little longer than planned because of a very wet winter.

The new library will open on the first of March, and the opening hours will be longer than before. From Monday to Friday we'll open from eight in the morning until eight at night, and on Saturdays from nine until five. We'll also open on Sundays, from ten until three, which has never been possible before.

The ground floor is for families. There's a large children's area with a storytelling corner, and a small cafe run by a local charity that trains young people in catering. On the first floor you'll find the main book collection, twenty computers, and quiet study pods, which you can reserve for up to two hours at a time. The top floor has a roof garden, which we hope will become a popular place to read in summer. We had thought of putting a gym there, but our surveys showed that residents preferred green space.

Membership is free for anyone living in the district. You'll need proof of address, such as a utility bill, when you sign up. You can borrow up to fifteen books at once, for three weeks, and renew them online. Books can be returned at any time, using the new lockers outside the main entrance.

We're also planning a program of events. Every Saturday morning there will be a coding club for ages nine to fourteen, and on Thursday evenings, a language exchange. Volunteers are still needed to help run these, so if you're interested, please speak to one of my colleagues at the desk by the door.

Finally, a word about getting here. There is no car park at the library itself, but the bus stop is just fifty meters from the entrance, and there are secure racks for two hundred bicycles. Thank you, and I hope to see you all on opening day.

items.q: Why did the council decide to build a new library instead of repairing the old one?
options: The old site was needed for a bus depot.
Repairs would have cost almost as much as a new building.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. So, how is your project on school start times coming along?
Quite well, Dr. Patel. We've decided to compare two schools in our region, one that starts at eight-thirty and one that starts at nine-thirty.
We wanted three schools at first, but only two principals replied to our emails.
That's common. Two is enough for a small study, as long as you are careful about what you claim. How will you collect the data?
We're going to use a questionnaire about sleep, given to about a hundred students at each school. Interviews would take too long.
But I'm worried that students may not remember accurately how long they slept. Maybe we should ask them to keep a diary for a week instead.

A diary is more reliable, but fewer students will complete it. A reasonable compromise would be a questionnaire for everyone and a diary for a small group, so that you can check the questionnaire results against it.
That makes sense. We'll do that.
And what results do you expect?
From our reading, we expect later starts to mean more sleep, but not necessarily better grades.
Yes, one earlier study found a small improvement in attendance, but test scores hardly changed at all.
Be careful with comparisons. Have you thought about differences between the two schools that have nothing to do with start time?
Well, the later school is in a wealthier area, so students there may have quieter bedrooms and more free time.
Exactly. You should mention that in your limitations section. I'd also collect information about travel time, because students who live far from school wake early whatever the start time is.
We hadn't thought of travel time. That's a good idea.
Now, the presentation. You have fifteen minutes. I suggest a short background first, and then spend most of the time on your method and findings. Use one graph per slide at the most.
Should we include a recommendation at the end?
Only if your data support it. If they don't, suggest further research instead. Send me a draft before the presentation and I'll give you feedback.

audio.t: Today I'd like to talk about bioluminescence, which means light produced by living things. Many people think of fireflies, but the greatest variety of glowing creatures lives in the deep ocean.

First, how does it work? The light comes from a chemical reaction. A molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, and the reaction is controlled by an enzyme called luciferase. Most light in the deep sea is blue, because blue light travels furthest through water, and many animals have eyes that are sensitive to it.

How common is it? Surveys of the open ocean suggest that about seventy-five percent of the animals living there can make their own light, or carry bacteria that do it for them. So it is the rule, not the exception.

Why do animals glow? There are three main reasons. The first is camouflage. Some squid and fish have small lights on the underside of the body. Seen from below, the lights match the faint sunlight coming from above, so the animal's shadow disappears. The second reason is hunting. The female anglerfish has a glowing lure that hangs in front of her mouth, and small fish swim toward it. The light is produced by bacteria that live inside the lure.

The third reason is defense. Some squid release a glowing cloud, which confuses a predator while the squid escapes into the dark. Other animals use what scientists call a burglar alarm. When attacked, they flash brightly, which attracts a larger predator, and that predator may then attack the first one.

You might also have seen bioluminescence near the shore. On warm summer nights, waves sometimes glow blue, because they contain millions of tiny plankton called dinoflagellates, which flash when the water around them moves.

Finally, bioluminescence is useful to humans. A glowing protein from a jellyfish is now used in laboratories to mark cells, so that scientists can watch what happens inside them. The discovery of this protein led to a Nobel Prize in 2008, and it has helped researchers to study diseases such as cancer. Next week, we'll look at how deep-sea animals cope with pressure.

items.text:
A
Citizen science, the involvement of non-professionals in scientific research, is often presented as a product of the internet age, yet its roots are much older. In 1900, an American ornithologist named Frank Chapman proposed that, instead of hunting birds on Christmas Day, as was then a popular tradition, people should count them. Twenty-seven observers took part in the first Christmas Bird Count. More than a century later, tens of thousands of volunteers join each year, and the accumulated records allow researchers to track how bird populations have shifted across a whole continent over generations, a task that no single laboratory could ever have afforded to carry out alone.

B
What digital technology changed was not the idea but its scale and speed. Smartphones carry cameras, GPS receivers and a constant internet connection, so a hiker who photographs an unfamiliar beetle can submit its location, the date and an image within seconds. Online platforms then allow other users, and increasingly machine-learning software, to suggest an identification, which experts can confirm or correct. In effect, a project can recruit thousands of observers without paying their wages or training them in person. The same technology has made it possible to collect observations at a density that would once have required an army of paid fieldworkers, and to do so continuously rather than during a single season.

C
Not all projects ask volunteers to go outdoors. In 2007, astronomers faced with a million images of galaxies, far more than a small team could classify in a lifetime, launched a website called Galaxy Zoo, which invited the public to sort galaxies by shape. Within a year, hundreds of thousands of people had contributed tens of millions of classifications. Unexpectedly, participants also drew attention to a group of small, unusually green galaxies that the automatic software had ignored and that the professional team had not noticed. Volunteers nicknamed them "peas", and they later became the subject of several scientific papers. The episode showed that human curiosity can sometimes find what a carefully designed program cannot.

D
Games offer another route into research. Foldit, launched in 2008, turned the problem of predicting how chains of protein fold into three-dimensional shapes into an online puzzle. Many players had no background in biology, yet their feel for spatial patterns sometimes beat the computer programs that scientists had written. In 2011, players helped to work out the structure of an enzyme from a monkey virus related to HIV, a puzzle that had resisted professional researchers for more than a decade. The players needed only a few weeks. Such results do not mean that experts are unnecessary, but they suggest that different kinds of thinking can complement each other.

E
Critics raise legitimate concerns. Volunteers tend to record what is easy and pleasant to observe: birds near roads and parks are heavily over-reported, while remote or unattractive places are neglected, so raw data can give a misleading picture of where species actually live. Identification mistakes are also common, especially among species that look alike, and a rare animal is more likely to be reported wrongly than a common one. Project designers have responded in several ways. They provide simple training materials, require photographs as evidence for unusual records, and use statistical methods that adjust for uneven observing effort. Some studies suggest that, when data are carefully checked, volunteers' records for well-defined tasks can come close to professional quality.

F
The benefits go beyond data. Participants often learn how science really works, including the uncertainty and slow checking that lie behind every conclusion, and some become advocates for protecting their local environment. Yet in many projects a small number of enthusiasts supply the majority of the records, while most people contribute only a handful of times and then drift away. The better programs therefore avoid treating volunteers as free labor. Several now invite participants to help shape the research questions, to co-author papers and to receive results in a form they can understand. The most successful collaborations, researchers argue, are those in which the public are treated as partners rather than as a supply of extra hands.

items.text:
A
Long before anyone understood germs, people had noticed that survivors of certain diseases rarely fell ill with the same disease twice. Smallpox, which killed perhaps three in every ten people it infected, was the most feared of all. Over many centuries, healers in parts of Asia, Africa and the Middle East deliberately exposed healthy people to material from smallpox sores, often by blowing dried scabs into the nose or scratching them into the skin, in the hope of provoking a mild case. This practice, known as variolation, was not without danger, since a small share of patients died, and some caught severe smallpox and passed it to others. Yet the odds were far better than those of catching the disease naturally, and the method reached Britain in the early eighteenth century, brought by travelers from the Ottoman Empire.

B
The decisive step came in 1796, when an English country doctor, Edward Jenner, tested a piece of local folk wisdom: that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild illness of cattle, did not catch smallpox. He took material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and introduced it into the arm of a young boy, and later exposed the boy to smallpox. The boy did not become ill. By modern standards the experiment was ethically unacceptable, but the underlying idea proved sound. The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow. Jenner's method was safer than variolation because cowpox could not cause smallpox, and it spread quickly across Europe and beyond, although it was met with suspicion by some, who feared that cow material would make people part animal.

C
The next major advance took almost a century, because scientists first needed a theory to explain why vaccination worked. In the 1860s and 1870s, the work of Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch established that specific microbes cause specific diseases. Pasteur then noticed, partly by accident, that cultures of the bacteria that cause chicken cholera lost their strength after being left on a shelf over a summer holiday, and that chickens injected with the weakened culture survived. He realized that weakened microbes could train the body to defend itself without causing severe illness. To honor Jenner, he applied the word vaccine to all such treatments. In 1885, Pasteur's team used a vaccine against rabies on a boy who had been bitten by a rabid dog, and the boy survived.

D
During the twentieth century, researchers developed several different strategies. Some vaccines contain living but weakened microbes, others contain microbes that have been killed, and others, such as those against diphtheria and tetanus, use a harmless form of the toxin that the bacteria produce. Polio shows how these approaches competed. In the 1940s and early 1950s, polio epidemics paralyzed thousands of children every summer. An injected vaccine made from killed viruses was announced in 1955, and an oral vaccine made from weakened viruses followed a few years later. The oral version was cheaper and could be given by volunteers with no medical training, which made it better suited to mass campaigns in poor countries, though in very rare cases the weakened virus could regain its strength.

E
The greatest success story is smallpox. In 1967, the World Health Organization launched an intensified campaign to remove the disease. Early efforts to vaccinate entire populations proved slow and expensive, so teams adopted a strategy known as ring vaccination: when a case was found, they traced the patient's contacts and vaccinated everyone around them, cutting the chain of infection. The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 the disease was declared eradicated. It remains the only human disease to have been removed in this way. A disease of cattle, rinderpest, was declared eradicated in 2011, showing that the approach can work for animals too.

F
Modern vaccine science faces new challenges. Developing a vaccine once took ten to fifteen years, but during the recent pandemic the first vaccines were authorized in less than a year. This speed was possible not because safety steps were skipped, but because the work built on decades of earlier research into a new technology, known as mRNA, which instructs the body's own cells to make a harmless piece of a virus. Hesitancy about vaccines is not new, however. Early nineteenth-century cartoons showed people sprouting cows from their bodies. Today, public trust depends on open communication, since vaccines protect not only the individual but also those who cannot be vaccinated, through so-called herd immunity. For a very infectious disease like measles, around ninety-five percent of the population needs to be immune before the chain of infection stops.

items.text:
A
Linguists estimate that around seven thousand languages are spoken in the world today, but they are very unevenly distributed. Fewer than four hundred languages have more than a million speakers each, whereas more than a third of the world's languages have fewer than a thousand. Roughly forty percent are considered endangered, which means that children are no longer learning them in large numbers. Many researchers predict that a large share of the total, perhaps half, will fall silent by the end of this century. It is important to understand what this means. Languages do not die in the way that living organisms do: they disappear when the last generation of speakers stops passing them on to its children.

B
The causes are seldom simple. Force alone is rarely the explanation; far more often the pressure is economic and social. Parents move from villages to cities in search of work, where a national or regional language dominates the market, the schools and the media. Many conclude, quite reasonably, that their children will have better opportunities if they speak the dominant language, and so they stop using their home language with them. In some regions, official policy accelerated the process. In parts of North America and Australia, for example, children were once punished for speaking their own languages at boarding schools, and a generation of adults grew up ashamed of the language of their grandparents.

C
Why does it matter? A language is more than a set of words for the same ideas; it is a store of knowledge built up over many generations. Languages spoken by small communities often contain detailed vocabulary for local plants, animals, weather and landscapes, some of which has never been written down in any other form. Certain Pacific languages, for instance, preserve techniques for navigating by stars and ocean swells. Linguists also value diversity for scientific reasons. Rare languages show how many different ways human grammar can work. Some require speakers to mark, in every sentence, how they know what they are saying, whether they saw it themselves or only heard about it. A theory of language based mainly on well-known languages would therefore be dangerously incomplete. Some economists argue that a world with fewer languages would be more efficient, but this overlooks the cultural value that the communities themselves attach to their speech.

D
The first response to a vanishing language is documentation. Field linguists record conversations, stories and songs, compile dictionaries and write grammars, often working with the last fluent speakers, who may be elderly and few in number. Digital archives now allow such recordings to be stored safely and shared with descendants who may wish to relearn the language. This work is urgent and valuable, but most researchers admit its limits. An archive can preserve a language as a record, yet it cannot make a language live. A language survives only when people use it to joke, argue, bargain and tell bedtime stories. As one researcher put it, a library of recordings is not a community.

E
There are encouraging examples of revival. In the late nineteenth century, Hebrew was used mainly for prayer and writing, not for everyday conversation, but within a few generations it became the daily language of millions of people. In New Zealand, the Maori language nests that began in 1982 were preschools in which fluent elders spoke only Maori with young children, so that the children absorbed the language as they played. The idea was later copied for Hawaiian, whose speakers had declined so far that few children could speak it, and immersion schools there have since produced a new generation of fluent young people. These programs share certain features: they begin with the youngest children, they involve the community, and they have strong political and financial support.

F
Technology is a double-edged tool. Keyboards and phones often fail to support the writing systems of small languages, and the most popular online services are available in only a few dozen. On the other hand, free apps, online dictionaries and text-prediction systems now allow communities to build their own resources cheaply, and some young speakers use their heritage language on social media as a mark of identity. Yet no tool replaces the basic requirement for survival. A language is kept alive less by gadgets than by the everyday decisions of families about what to speak at home. Revival is slow and uncertain, and its success depends on whether a language can offer its speakers a real purpose in daily life.

items.text:
The table shows the percentage of workers in the town of Calderbrook who used four different ways of travelling to work in 2000, 2010 and 2020.

Car: 68 (2000), 61 (2010), 52 (2020)
Bus or train: 20 (2000), 22 (2010), 24 (2020)
Bicycle: 4 (2000), 7 (2010), 12 (2020)
On foot: 8 (2000), 10 (2010), 12 (2020)

Note: a new bicycle lane network opened in the town center in 2012.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares how workers in Calderbrook traveled to their jobs in 2000, 2010 and 2020. Overall, the car remained the most common choice throughout the period, but its share fell steadily, while every other method became more popular.

In 2000, more than two thirds of workers, 68 percent, drove to work. This figure dropped to 61 percent in 2010 and then to 52 percent in 2020, a fall of 16 percentage points. Even so, the car was still used by roughly half of all workers at the end of the period.

Public transport was the second most popular option in every year. The proportion of people using buses or trains grew slowly, from 20 percent to 22 percent and finally to 24 percent. By contrast, the two active methods grew faster in relative terms. Cycling tripled, from only 4 percent in 2000 to 12 percent in 2020, and the biggest rise came after the bicycle lane network opened in 2012. Walking increased more modestly, from 8 percent to 12 percent, so that by 2020 cycling and walking were used by the same share of workers.

In summary, Calderbrook workers moved gradually away from private cars toward public transport and, above all, toward cycling and walking.

items.q: Some people believe that working from home is better for both employees and employers. Others think that employees should work in an office with their colleagues. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
items.sample:
People disagree about whether work is best done at home or in an office. Although working remotely has clear advantages, I believe that the strongest arrangement combines both.

Supporters of home working make several fair points. Employees save the time and money they would otherwise spend on commuting, and many report that they can concentrate better without the interruptions of a busy office. This can improve their health and their satisfaction with life, which in turn makes them more likely to stay with a company. Employers also benefit, because they can employ people who live far away and may need smaller and cheaper buildings.

However, those who prefer the office also have a strong case. Face-to-face contact makes it easier to build trust, share ideas informally and solve problems quickly. New employees in particular learn a great deal simply by watching more experienced colleagues, and this kind of learning is hard to copy through a screen. In addition, some people live in small or noisy homes where it is difficult to work, and they may feel isolated if they spend weeks without seeing another person.

In my opinion, neither extreme is ideal. A flexible model, in which staff spend two or three days a week in the office and the rest at home, keeps the benefits of both. Meetings, training and team projects can be planned for office days, while tasks that need quiet concentration are done at home. Companies should also let employees help to decide the pattern that suits their roles.

In conclusion, working from home offers freedom and efficiency, but the office offers connection and support, so a balance between the two is the wisest solution for most organizations.

items.q: Describe a teacher who helped you to learn something important. You should say: who the teacher was, what he or she taught you, how he or she helped you, and explain why this teacher was important to you.
items.sample:
I would like to talk about my English teacher from secondary school, Mrs. Lan, who helped me more than any other teacher. She taught me English for three years, but she also taught me how to study, which is the most important thing I learned at school.

When I first joined her class, I was very shy and afraid of making mistakes, so I almost never spoke. Mrs. Lan noticed this and did not force me. Instead, she gave me small tasks, like reading one sentence aloud or answering a simple question, and she always smiled and said that mistakes are a normal part of learning. Slowly, I became more confident. She also showed me practical methods, such as keeping a notebook of new words and listening to short songs every day.

By the end of the first year, I could introduce myself to a group of strangers without feeling nervous, and my grades improved a lot. She also encouraged me to join the English club, where I made some of my best friends.

This teacher was important to me because she changed the way I think about difficult things. I learned that patience and regular practice are more useful than talent. Even now, when I face a hard problem, I remember her advice and try to take it one small step at a time. I am very grateful to her.
