audio.t: Good evening everyone, and thank you for coming to this meeting about the Eastgate Community Orchard. I am the project coordinator, and tonight I will explain how the scheme will work and how you can take part.

First, some background. The orchard will be planted on the old bus depot, which has stood empty for nearly ten years. The council's first plan was to build a car park there, but a petition signed by more than eight hundred residents persuaded them to choose something greener. The council also looked at building a sports hall, but that would have cost far more.

The site is smaller than you might expect, about half a hectare, so we have chosen dwarf varieties. In total there will be sixty trees, mostly apple and plum, with a few pear. Many people ask about cherries, but they grow tall and wide, and they would block the light for the vegetable beds, so we have left them out. Birds are not a concern, as we will use nets.

Planting day is the first Saturday of March. We need about forty volunteers, and no experience is required, because trained gardeners will show you what to do. We will provide all the tools and a hot drink, but please bring a pair of gloves, as we only have a few spare. There is no need to bring lunch, as the food bank will provide sandwiches.

Once the trees are established, the harvest will be shared. Half goes to the volunteers, a quarter to the local food bank, and the rest will be sold at the Sunday market to pay for maintenance. We did think about giving some fruit to schools, but the paperwork was too complicated.

Alongside the orchard, we are opening a tool library in the old ticket office. Most households use a ladder or a drill only a few times a year, so the idea is that people borrow what they need instead of buying it. It will help people avoid spending money on things that then sit in a cupboard. Teaching repair skills is not the main aim, and the library will not make a profit.
Membership costs twelve dollars a year, but only five dollars for students and retired people.
The tool library will open on Wednesday and Saturday. We hoped to open on Tuesday too, but we do not have enough volunteers yet, and Sunday is reserved for the market.

We also plan a monthly repair cafe, where experts help you mend broken items for free. The first one, next month, will deal with bicycles, because so many people asked for it. Clothing and small appliances will follow later in the year.

A word about getting there. There is no parking on the site, and the car park near the station is a ten-minute walk away. My advice is to take the number fourteen bus, which stops right at the gate. There are some cycle racks too, though they are rather few at the moment.

Finally, if you would like to volunteer, please register on the orchard website. We cannot take names by phone, and the ticket office will not be open until the tool library starts. Thank you, and I am happy to take questions now.

audio.t: Come in, both of you. I have read your outline for the energy storage project. First, tell me how you chose the topic.
It started with my uncle. He put solar panels on his roof last year, but he still loses power in the evening, because he cannot store what the panels make during the day.
And I had read that old batteries from electric cars still hold most of their capacity, so we wondered whether they could be reused in homes.
A good question. My main worry is the scope. At the moment your outline covers the whole world, and you only have four thousand words. I would choose one country.
We will stick to our own country, then.
Sensible. What are you using as your main source?
A report from the National Energy Institute. It has plenty of figures on costs.
Good, but check the date. Battery prices have fallen so fast that figures more than three years old can be misleading.
I will look at the publication date and find something newer if I need to.
And how will you collect your own data?
We first planned a survey of homeowners, but nobody we know has actually installed this type of system. We cannot test batteries in a laboratory either, so interviews with installers seem best.
I agree. Have you made contact yet?
We emailed twenty installers last week and only two have replied.
That is not unusual. I would not offer payment, but you could ask their trade association to forward your request. People tend to answer a message from their own organization.
Good idea. I also want a section on safety, because people worry about fires.
Definitely keep it. It is the first thing readers will ask about, and it shows you have thought about the risks.
One more thing. I have drawn a graph of battery prices over time, with five lines for different battery types.
It is too crowded. I would cut it down to two lines, the ones you actually compare.
Fine. And for the cost comparison, I thought of putting it in an appendix to save space.
I would not. It is your key result, so present it in a table in the main text, and keep the appendix for the raw data.
Right. When is the draft due? I thought it was the twentieth.
The twentieth was the old date. Your draft is due on the twelfth, and the final version on the twenty-seventh.
That is sooner than I expected.
So what will you do first?
I will email the trade association this afternoon, and Callum will redraw the graph.
Excellent. Come back to me when you have some replies.

audio.t: Today I want to look at how lighthouse technology developed, because it is a neat example of engineering solving a very practical problem.

The earliest lighthouses, built beside ancient Mediterranean ports, simply burned wood on top of a tower. The trouble was that the wind scattered the sparks and the smoke hid the flame, so sailors often could not tell a lighthouse from the glow of a village.
By the seventeenth century many towers used coal, which burned hotter than wood, but it needed a worker to feed the fire all night, and the cost of carrying fuel up the tower was high.

A big step came in the 1780s, when an inventor called Lucien Marsac designed a lamp with a hollow circular wick. Air could reach the flame from inside as well as outside, and the result was a light about ten times brighter than a normal candle flame.

But a bright lamp is not much use unless the light is sent in one direction. Early reflectors were made from copper coated with silver, but they quickly tarnished in the salty air and lost much of their brightness, so keepers had to polish them every day.

The real breakthrough came in the 1820s, when a French physicist built a lens from rings of glass prisms. Instead of one thick lump of glass, the lens used many thin pieces to bend the light into a single beam. A large lens of this kind could be seen from twenty miles away, and it was far lighter than any earlier design.
Fuel changed too. Oil lamps replaced coal, and then in the early 1900s electric bulbs took over from oil in many towers. That removed the daily job of trimming wicks.

Today most lighthouses are fully automatic. Nobody lives in the tower; engineers visit only for repairs, and many lights are monitored from a control room on shore. Next week, we will look at what this means for the way sailors find their way using satellites.

items.text:
Smart Cities and the Price of Privacy
A. When the city of Orlund installed four thousand sensors on its streets in 2019, officials described the project as a quiet revolution. Bins that signal when they are full, lamps that dim when nobody is walking beneath them, and traffic lights that adjust to the flow of cars were expected to cut both costs and pollution. Within three years, the energy used for street lighting had fallen by about a third, and the average bus journey was nine percent faster. Yet the same network that counted cars also counted people, and by 2022 residents had begun to ask what else it recorded, who could see it, and how long it was kept.
B. Such questions are not unique to Orlund. The term "smart city" covers any urban area that uses connected devices to collect data and improve services, and the data is rarely used for one purpose only. A camera installed to detect illegal parking can, after a software update, be made to recognize faces. A transport card that speeds up payment also records where its owner travels each day, and a pattern of journeys can reveal a person's workplace, friends and even regular medical visits. Researchers call this "function creep": a system built for a modest aim gradually acquires new uses that citizens never agreed to, and that the original designers may not have intended.
C. Defenders of smart systems stress that most of the data is anonymous. In Orlund, the sensors record only that a person passed, not who it was. Privacy scholars reply that anonymity is more fragile than it sounds. In a well-known experiment, a university team showed that just four points in time and place taken from a phone's location history were enough to single out the great majority of individuals in a data set of more than a million people. When data sets from different sources are combined, even names that have been removed can often be restored, and a determined analyst needs little more than patience and a second spreadsheet.
D. A second concern is who holds the data. Many cities lack the technical staff to run such networks, so they sign contracts with private companies. In Orlund, the contract allowed the supplier to keep "aggregated" data for product development. Councillors had approved the contract in a single short meeting, and few of them understood that clause. Critics argue that when public streets become sources of commercial information, residents are paying twice: once with their taxes and once with their data. Supporters answer that without private expertise the savings would never have been achieved, and that public ownership of every system is unrealistic for all but the largest cities.
E. Several cities have tried a middle path. Kestrel Bay publishes a register of every sensor, stating its purpose, the data it collects and the date on which that data will be deleted. Residents can search the register on a map and challenge any entry; since the register opened, eleven devices have been removed. Another approach, used in the town of Dunmere, is known as "privacy by design". Its cameras process images inside the device and send only a count of pedestrians, never a picture, to the central system. Engineers admit that this costs about fifteen percent more per unit, but they say it avoids the need to store sensitive material that could be hacked or misused.
F. Not everyone is convinced that such measures go far enough. A citizens' panel in Orlund, chosen by lottery, spent six weekends reviewing the project and concluded that the sensors should stay, but that collection should be limited to what is needed to deliver each service. The panel also proposed an independent auditor with the power to inspect the system and publish findings. The council accepted the second idea but postponed the first, arguing that detailed limits would slow down improvements. Observers note that the debate has shifted. Few people now ask whether cities should be smart; the question is whether they can stay accountable once they are. As one panel member put it, a city's intelligence is worth little if its residents are the last to know what it knows.

items.text:
Rebuilding the Reef
A. Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. They also protect coastlines by absorbing wave energy, and they support fisheries and tourism that provide a living for hundreds of millions of people. When marine heatwaves caused repeated bleaching across the tropics, reducing the living coral on some reefs by more than half within a single decade, the response from scientists was urgent. Protecting reefs from further harm was no longer enough; some argued that damaged reefs would need active help to recover.
B. The oldest restoration method is also the simplest. Divers break healthy corals into small fragments, attach them to frames in a nursery in calm water, and wait. Many species grow fast after being broken, because each fragment treats the break as an injury and repairs it by growing. After about a year, the fragments are fixed to a damaged reef with cement or cable ties. At Lantern Reef, a nursery run by marine biologist Ines Varga has planted more than forty thousand fragments. Yet she is careful about the results. "We can grow coral quickly," she says. "What we cannot yet do is rebuild the whole reef community, with its fish, sponges and worms, at the same speed."
C. A weakness of fragment planting is genetic sameness. Fragments cut from one colony are clones, and clones share the same weaknesses, so a single disease or a spell of hot water can wipe out an entire planted patch. Newer projects therefore collect fragments from many colonies and favor those that survived heatwaves. A team in the Sarrow Islands tests nursery corals in warm tanks, selects those that tolerate water two degrees above normal, and plants only these. Critics worry that breeding for heat tolerance may reduce other useful traits, but early field results are encouraging: selected corals lost about half as much living tissue in a heatwave as unselected neighbors.
D. A second approach works with reproduction rather than against it. Once a year, on a few nights after a full moon, many corals release eggs and sperm into the water at the same time. Scientists collect this cloud of material in floating nets, allow fertilization to happen under controlled conditions, and raise the larvae in tanks before returning them to the reef as tiny settlers. Because the offspring are genetically new, this method creates diversity that fragmenting cannot. Its drawback is cost and scale. Each larva is a fragile thing, and only a very small fraction survive long enough to settle and grow on the reef.
E. Larvae will only settle on a clean, suitable surface, and in recent years researchers have realized that sound matters. Healthy reefs are noisy places, filled with the crackles of snapping shrimp and the grunts of fish, whereas dead reefs are almost silent. In an experiment at Calder Shoal, speakers playing recordings of a healthy reef were placed on degraded patches. Over six weeks, twice as many young fish arrived at those patches as at silent control sites. Supporters say that sound could attract the fish that clean algae from corals; skeptics point out that it does nothing about the heat that killed the reef in the first place.
F. This last objection runs through the whole field. Restoration cannot succeed for long if the causes of damage remain, and the largest cause is warming seas. Many scientists therefore treat restoration as a way of buying time rather than a cure. Their reasoning is that a restored patch can keep a local ecosystem alive, protect a shoreline and preserve genetic stock while the world works to reduce the emissions that heat the oceans. Others warn that visible success stories may weaken the pressure for such action, creating a false sense that the problem can simply be repaired.
G. Cost is also a factor. Fragment planting is cheap on a small scale, but when it is extended to a whole reef it becomes expensive. A recent review estimated that restoring a single hectare could cost anywhere from a few thousand to several hundred thousand dollars, depending on the method, the depth and the distance from shore. Local communities are increasingly central to the work: on Sarrow, fishers are paid to tend nurseries, which gives them an income and a reason to defend the reef. Varga believes this may matter more than any technique. "A reef with people who depend on it," she says, "is a reef that will be looked after long after the scientists have left."

items.text:
The Psychology of Habit
A. Studies of everyday behavior suggest that a large share of what people do each day is repeated in the same setting, with little conscious thought. Psychologists define a habit not as a frequent action but as an automatic response triggered by context. A person who reaches for a phone on sitting down on the train has a habit; a person who decides each morning to go for a run is merely persistent. The distinction matters, because it explains why habits survive moments of weak motivation and why they can continue even when people no longer want the outcome.
B. A widely used model describes a habit loop with three parts: a cue, a routine and a reward. The cue, which might be a time, a place, a feeling or the presence of other people, prompts the routine, and the reward then strengthens the link between the two. Over many repeated cycles, control of the behavior shifts from brain regions involved in deliberate choice toward deeper structures that handle automatic sequences. Experiments on rats running through mazes show this change. At first, brain activity is high throughout the run; after training, activity peaks only at the start and the end, as if the animal had packaged the whole sequence into a single unit.
C. A popular belief holds that it takes twenty-one days to form a habit. In fact, there is no firm basis for this figure. One study followed ninety-six volunteers who each chose a new daily behavior, such as eating fruit at lunch or doing a short exercise routine, and recorded how automatic it felt. The time required ranged from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days, with a typical value of about sixty-six. Simple actions became automatic sooner than complex ones, and missing a single day did no lasting damage. The lesson is that the pace of change varies enormously between people and between behaviors.
D. Context is a more powerful ally than willpower. Researchers who tracked students moving to a new university found that habits tied to the old environment, such as watching a particular television program, weakened after the move, and that the students were then more likely to start new behaviors that matched their intentions. This helps to explain why changing jobs or moving house can be a rare opportunity for change. It also supports the advice to redesign surroundings: placing fruit on the counter and putting biscuits in a high cupboard makes the desired behavior easier. Such small changes cost little, yet in workplace canteens, moving healthy options to eye level has shifted choices more than posters encouraging healthy eating.
E. Bad habits are harder. The usual advice is to resist, but suppression often fails because the cue remains and the old routine is still stored in memory. A better strategy is substitution: keep the cue and the reward, but alter the routine. Someone who snacks at a desk at three o'clock may be seeking a break and a little company rather than food, and a short walk to talk to a colleague can satisfy the same need. Therapists who treat nervous habits, such as nail biting, teach clients a "competing response", a harmless movement that cannot be done at the same time as the habit, to practice whenever the urge arises. Success rates are good, though relapse under stress is common.
F. Critics of the habit approach warn against overselling. Some behaviors, such as saving money or following a medication schedule, involve decisions that vary from day to day and cannot become automatic in the same way. Others, like exercise, depend on circumstances that change with the weather, the season or a person's health. There is also evidence that people who attribute their success wholly to habit may feel helpless when a habit breaks, believing they have lost their system. Researchers increasingly favor plans that combine automatic routines with flexible, deliberate decisions: a fixed time and place for exercise, for instance, with several options for what to do there.
G. Digital technology has added a new dimension. Apps that send notifications, display streaks and reward small actions with points borrow directly from the habit loop. Designers say this helps users build healthy behaviors, from drinking water to studying a language. But the same techniques are used to hold attention on social media, where cues arrive constantly and rewards are unpredictable, a pattern that research shows to be especially strong at sustaining a behavior. Ethicists suggest that the difference between supporting a user's own goals and exploiting their impulses should be the test of whether a design is acceptable.

parts.instr: WRITING TASK 1. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.
parts.instrVi: BÀI VIẾT 1. Nên dành khoảng 20 phút cho bài này.

items.text:
The table shows the average time, in minutes, that workers spent commuting each day in four countries in 2005 and in 2025, and the percentage of workers in each country who worked from home at least one day a week in 2025.
Norland: 48 minutes in 2005; 41 minutes in 2025; 34% worked from home.
Estavia: 62 minutes in 2005; 71 minutes in 2025; 18% worked from home.
Brisca: 35 minutes in 2005; 33 minutes in 2025; 52% worked from home.
Tamora: 54 minutes in 2005; 58 minutes in 2025; 25% worked from home.
items.q: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
items.sample:
The table compares daily commuting times in four countries in 2005 and 2025, and shows how many workers were working from home at least once a week in 2025. Overall, commuting became shorter in the two countries with the most remote working, while it became longer in the two countries where fewer people worked from home.
Brisca had the shortest commute in both years, falling slightly from 35 to 33 minutes, and it also had the highest share of home workers, at 52%. Norland followed a similar pattern. Its commute fell from 48 to 41 minutes, a drop of seven minutes, and just over a third of its workers (34%) worked from home.
In contrast, Estavia had the longest commute in both years, and the time increased from 62 to 71 minutes, the biggest rise in the table. It also recorded the lowest figure for home working, at only 18%. Tamora lay between the two groups: its commute rose by four minutes to 58, and a quarter of its workers (25%) worked from home. In summary, the countries with more flexible working tended to see shorter journeys.

parts.instr: WRITING TASK 2. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task.

items.q: Some people believe that university students should study only subjects that will help them find a job. Others believe that students should be free to study whatever interests them. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
items.sample:
Universities exist to educate young people, but there is disagreement about what that education should include. Some people argue that students should choose only subjects that lead to employment, while others believe they should follow their interests. In my opinion, both approaches have value, and the best choice depends on balance.
Supporters of job-focused study make a reasonable point. Tuition is expensive, and many students borrow money to pay for it. Graduates in fields such as engineering, nursing or computing usually find work quickly, and governments also benefit when there are enough trained people to fill essential roles. A student who ignores the labor market may graduate with debts and few opportunities, which can be a heavy burden.
However, there are strong arguments for studying what interests you. Students who enjoy a subject tend to work harder, achieve better results and stay motivated for the whole course. Moreover, the job market changes quickly, and some of the occupations that will exist in twenty years do not exist today. Subjects such as history, philosophy or languages develop skills like critical thinking, writing and communication that employers value in almost every field. A curious graduate may adapt more easily than one who trained narrowly for a single job.
I believe the most sensible approach is a combination. Students should consider their career goals, but they should not choose a course they dislike simply because it seems safe. Universities can help by offering flexible degrees in which students combine a practical subject with one they love, and by providing careers advice from the first year. In this way, young people can prepare for work without losing the curiosity that makes learning worthwhile.
In conclusion, studying for a job and studying for interest are not opposites. A balanced choice gives students the best chance of both a secure career and a satisfying one.

parts.instr: Part 1. Answer the examiner's questions about familiar topics.
parts.instrVi: Phần 1. Trả lời các câu hỏi về chủ đề quen thuộc.

items.q: What do you like most about the area where you live?
items.sample: What I like most about my neighborhood is that it is very friendly. Everyone knows each other, and there is a small park nearby because the council built it last year.
items.vi: Nói điều em thích nhất ở nơi mình sống, kèm lý do.

items.q: How do you usually travel around your town?
items.sample: I usually travel by bus because it is cheap and there is a stop near my house. When the weather is nice, I sometimes ride my bike to save time.
items.vi: Nói phương tiện thường dùng và lý do.

items.q: Do you enjoy cooking? Why or why not?
items.sample: Yes, I really enjoy cooking because it helps me relax after school. I often make simple dishes with my mother, and I would like to learn more recipes.
items.vi: Trả lời có/không về việc nấu ăn và giải thích.

items.q: How do you like to spend your weekends?
items.sample: At the weekend I usually do my homework on Saturday morning. In the afternoon I meet my friends, and on Sunday we often visit my grandparents for lunch.
items.vi: Kể cách em dành cuối tuần.

parts.instr: Part 2. Talk about the topic on the card for one to two minutes.
parts.instrVi: Phần 2. Nói về chủ đề trên thẻ trong 1-2 phút.

items.q: Describe a skill you learned that you are proud of. You should say: what the skill is; how you learned it; who helped you; and explain why you are proud of it.
items.sample: I would like to talk about swimming, which is a skill I learned when I was eleven. I am quite proud of it because I was afraid of deep water for a long time. I learned it at the community pool near my school, where a coach ran lessons every Saturday morning. At first I could only float for a few seconds, and I felt embarrassed because younger children were swimming faster than me. My coach was very patient. She taught me to breathe properly and to relax my arms, and she always said that small steps were better than rushing. My father also helped by taking me to the pool on Sundays to practice. After about four months, I could swim a whole length without stopping. Later I joined the school team and took part in a small competition. I did not win, but finishing the race made me very happy. I am proud of this skill because I learned it slowly and I had to face a real fear. It also taught me that I can improve at almost anything if I practice regularly and do not give up.

parts.instr: Part 3. Discuss these more abstract questions with the examiner.

items.q: Why do some people find it hard to learn new skills as adults?
items.sample: I think adults often find it hard because they have less free time than children. They work and look after their families, so they cannot practice every day. Many adults also have a fear of looking foolish, and that fear stops them from trying.
items.vi: Giải thích vì sao người lớn khó học kỹ năng mới: ít thời gian, sợ mắc lỗi.

items.q: Should schools teach practical skills as well as academic subjects?
items.sample: Yes, I think schools should teach practical skills. For example, students could learn how to manage money, cook simple meals or give first aid. These skills are useful for daily life, and they can help young people feel more confident when they leave school.
items.vi: Nêu ý kiến về việc dạy kỹ năng thực hành ở trường, có ví dụ.

items.q: How might technology change the way people learn in the future?
items.sample: In the future, technology will probably make learning more personal. Perhaps students will use programs that notice their weak points and give them extra practice. People may also learn new skills at any age, because online courses and virtual classrooms will be available everywhere.
items.vi: Dự đoán công nghệ thay đổi việc học: cá nhân hóa, học mọi lúc mọi nơi.
